We investigate the eigenspectra of large, randomly constructed Hermitian block matrices, whose structure is perturbed by a finite rank complex modification. Given that the band's width expands faster than the square root of the matrix's size, our analysis demonstrates that the statistical distribution of the imaginary components of the eigenvectors aligns with the results from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. This finding was achieved using the methods and approaches developed in the arXiv paper, 1802.03813. In our work, we verify the methods and approaches by comparing them with existing findings. This verification involves showing the approximate equality of the corrected spectral density at the band's edge, calculated both perturbatively and within the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble, to be less than a certain small value. Following this verification, our analysis demonstrates that the calculated spectral density serves as a continuous field theory. Our approaches and methods are also applied to general transformations of the eigenspectra, rather than just the imaginary components, and the associated distributions have been calculated. This has led to the demonstration that the time reversal symmetric Gaussian Unitary Ensemble is equivalent to the Haar measure on the space of symmetric matrices whose eigenvalues lie close together. Calculations of the imaginary components and the distributions of the eigenvectors, for various sizes of the matrix's rank, have also been performed numerically. These calculations validate our analytical findings and demonstrate the methods' and approaches' effectiveness. Our work, although grounded in theoretical approaches, has been supported by numerical results, which verify our analytical findings and validate the effectiveness of the methods and approaches. All data used in our work was generated numerically, providing further evidence of the validity of the results. Our analysis extends existing theories and approaches, which were initially developed for real transformations, to their complex counterparts. We have thoroughly discussed the theoretical and numerical results, connecting them to existing theories, such as disorder-free symmetry-protected topological phases and the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. Our work has been performed completely away from numerical renormalization group, utilizing an over-complete basis to study the model, which aligns with the description of the disorder-free SPT phase. We have also discussed the relationship between the smooth extension of the density of states and the f-matrix, which describes the distribution of the eigenstates. Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, models reliant on surface-level dialogue text struggle to comprehend dialogue context, particularly in extracting the underlying semantic meaning. In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we introduce the use of Abstract Meaning Representation as a means of pre-training language models with explicit semantic information, which captures the essence of dialogue during the pre-training phase. Building upon the standard pre-training framework, we formulate a semantic-based pre-training approach that includes three key tasks: learning core semantic units, semantic relations, and overall semantic representation. Empirical results from the analysis of casual and task-based conversations confirm the superiority of our proposed model over traditional approaches. Furthermore, we contribute a novel paradigm by integrating pre-trained semantic representations into a variety of dialogue applications, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing model performance. The corresponding code is made available on our GitHub page at https://github.com/allenai/SEM4C. Moreover, we release our built-in dialogue understanding validation set, known as the SEM4C-baseline benchmark on https://allenaipublic.github.io/SEM4C-baseline. Please note that our model's performance is still based on automatic evaluations and a comprehensive human evaluation is recommended for assessing the model's quality in real-world applications. The model's performance details can also be found on our AllenAI public page at https://allenai.github.io/SEM4C-baseline/evaluation. The model's performance can be evaluated by clicking the 'Run' button. The model supports Spanish and English languages. The model's parameters were set as follows: max dialog turn is 10, core sentence count is 5, and the MNI vector size is 1024. The model was trained for 24 hours on a Tesla V100 GPU. The model's performance is mainly attributed to the use of various dialogue-specific resources such as the UIMA Semantic basses of English and Spanish, the Probase graph, and the BERT4TOX embedding model, which enables the use of a pre-trained transformer-based model. The model also uses a variety of soft and hard attention techniques including BERT, BART, BUE, DRAGON, and GPT-3. The model's predicted semantic representation can serve as an effective dialogue understanding solution that complements existing dialogue generation models. To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as hold developers accountable, algorithmic interpretability must be measured. This study draws on principles from programming languages and learning theory to establish a comprehensive framework for assessing interpretability. This proposed method captures the essence of how a person learns an algorithm, and through rigorous evaluation, we prove its advantages in four key areas - it applies universally, can be computed easily, yields distinct results, and accurately tracks increasing complexity. By presenting the framework through a hypothetical scenario and detailing its practical application, we demonstrate its efficacy in evaluating a range of algorithms from simple to complex, such as Sine and Logistical Regression, as well as others employing surprise and long short-term memory. Furthermore, our method is cost-efficient and requires minimal resources, making it a viable solution for large and complex algorithms, ultimately contributing to the development of a trainable, self-improving algorithmic interpretability standard. Self-improvement in this context means the system modifies its own metric or goal without human intervention for enhanced performance. This research brings together the principles of programming languages, algorithmic learning theory, and advances in reinforcement learning for a groundbreaking approach to algorithmic interpretability, ultimately contributing to the evolution of a trainable, self-improving standard. As a result, we propose a new benchmark based on these principles, offering a quantitative method to gauge the complexity of algorithms from simple to sophisticated, such as those used in surprise and long short-term memory. This study is a significant contribution to the evolution of algorithmic interpretability, ultimately resulting in the development of a trainable, self-improving standard. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a specific nonlinear function, which is shown to have a posterior distribution that remains unchanged under Markov-Chain Monte-Carlo simulations. This technique is accompanied by an approximation ensuring the exact preservation of the original posterior's marginal distribution. This method's efficiency is demonstrated in an simulation study comparing it with another Bayesian approach, which uses adaptive Markov-Chain Monte-C Carl techniques. Finally, we apply this method to real-world data, analysing extreme drought in Spain and extreme rainfall in the UK. This method can be accessed through the R package poislmi.

This analysis addresses the challenge in average cross section calculations, arising from its definition as an average of cross section values at different points. To overcome this issue, the approach involves treating the cross section as a function, and its argument as a variable. The problem is then transformed into determining the stationary points of this cross section function. The paper makes two key contributions. Firstly, it identifies the conditions necessary for stationary points in any cross section. Secondly, it provides specific criteria for deriving such points in the case of average cross section calculations, involving fission product distributions. Utilizing these principles, the authors apply them to a model system, analyzing a trimolecular reaction and obtaining results that could be relevant to understanding neutron-induced reactions in xenon-135, particularly for improving nuclear reactor safety by mitigating a hypothetical chain reaction initiated by a neutron parallel to 135I. The study shows that for a certain xenon isotope, the average cross section exhibits negative values in response to neutron energy, a behavior that may be responsible for a monotonically decreasing fission probability in a narrow range of this neutron energy. The origin of this negative value lies in the weakly elastic nature of the reaction, where a slight increase in the final neutron energy results in a significant negative contribution due to the energy disparity between the incoming and remaining neutrons. Furthermore, for a different xenon isotope, the average cross section exhibits the U-shaped pattern characteristic of a double resonance phenomenon, a consequence of two distinct energy ranges among which neutron energy switches. The specific ranges are found to be those where a double resonance occurs on a particular isotope of xenon-136 and a neighboring isotope. In summary, this investigation emphasizes the necessity of understanding the behavior of average cross sections, highlighting instances where this average exhibits unusual patterns, such as negative values or a double resonance shape. The study also emphasizes the importance of and facilitating approaches to detect such behaviors in actual neutron-induced reactions, particularly to prevent a chain reaction in reactors and prevent a collapse of a particle detector's accuracy due to an unusually large cross section. The particular applications of this research involve a significant role in a variety of fields, including low-abundance isotope separation and medical treatment. To guide future advancements, we've identified areas of improvement required to surpass the symbol-based COMET-ATOMIC 202 dataset, and we've explored potential avenues for increasing its utility. We introduce the data processing pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey. This critical component is an integral part of the Herschel satellite project that's mapping the Galactic plane's inner regions. Leveraging a combination of Herschel Interactive Standard Environment capabilities and new, custom-designed tools, our pipeline effectively handles data reduction tasks. In modeling systems of rival agents as games, assuming each party makes rational decisions, the probable outcomes can be identified using equilibrium concepts like the Nash equilibrium. In various real-world scenarios, factors like weather, traffic or fiscal policy, beyond the agents' control, can impact game dynamics. Often, the equilibrium observed doesn't align with the actual cost functions of the models representing the agents. This research proposes the use of Nash Fixed Point Networks, a new family of neural networks, capable of predicting game equilibria through actual observed outcomes, without needing access to game-specific details like source code, the game's mathematical structure, or player lists. NFPNs are based on the idea that known equilibrium detection methods can be viewed as solving a specific problem, and by applying this perspective, NFPNs break down non-convex problems involving many variables into more manageable local components, and improve iteratively with each layer. NFPNs' effectiveness is shown through actual results on several complex games where they accurately predict different types of equilibria including the circling traffic, Bertrand, and linear matching games, and they anticipate the impact of external factors in circling traffic and matching games. This technique has broad potential as it can operate without a complete understanding of a game's internal workings, and can also be adapted for other type of predictions beyond equilibria, such as predicting a game's payoff. Furthermore, we achieve a categorical equivalence between the category of one-dimensional S-rings of Krull type and the category of sets, where the objects in this equivalence correspond to sets of prime ideals within a specific ring of formal power series. As a result, it follows that every one-dimensional S-ring of Krull type can be expressed as a quotient of a ring of formal power series, where the equivalence is based on the given set of prime ideals. Moreover, a specific duality theorem is developed to relate the characteristics of prime ideals within one-dimensional S-rings of Krull type to those of prime ideals within dual pseudo-Shah diagrams. Recently, Variation Autoencoders have emerged as a preferred choice for unsupervised learning of intricate probability distributions. Compared to traditional autoencoders, VAEs exhibit enhanced reconstructive capabilities, making more accurate approximations of probability distributions possible, especially in intricate scenarios. However, VAEs face challenges in providing a precise fit to complex distributions, often resulting in poor reconstructive performances and unstable training experiences. To address these challenges, a thorough theoretical examination of Bayes' rule-derived loss functions was conducted, leading to a novel finding that conventional functions can be imperfect and biased. To improve generalization, a regularization technique was proposed, based on a minimum square error approach that detects overestimation/underestimation disparities in the mean and variance. By achieving such a discovery, training difficulties related to unstable gradients could be overcome through derivative calculations. The proposed approach demonstrated superior performance on various benchmark datasets when compared to established competitors. Moreover, the empirical analysis revealed a significant improvement in the learning dynamics, including lower gradient magnitudes and increased runtime. This research contributes to filling this need by designing an affordable, network security system utilizing a private blockchain and a location tracking technique based on wireless signal strength. Our investigation highlights the benefits of private blockchains and optimizes the location tracking accuracy by testing its performance with various wireless networks. The results demonstrate that integrating a private blockchain with Wi-Fi technology achieves the best results for our proposed system. Moreover, our experimental analysis shows that incorporating a private blockchain increases network throughput by 30%, reduces energy consumption by 25%, and enhances data safety with enhanced SHA-256 hash code uniqueness, resulting in a 3.8x improvement. This results in a strong foundation for ensuring smart home device security. The results also reveal that wireless networks other options like Ethernet and Gigabit Ethernet, while secure, fail to meet our performance requirements. Finally, our assessment of the computational overhead shows that deploying a private blockchain in the smart home network has a minimal effect on performance, meeting our criteria for throughput and energy consumption. The results suggest that deploying private blockchains in constrained systems may be feasible after optimizing the storage layer for database files, which led to a 7.0 KB and 2.1 KB reduction in file size for Ethereum and private blockchain, respectively. It was discovered that average L-values of QAM symbols consistently adhere to an ordered relationship, a property overlooked in previous research. Leveraging this finding, a deep learning-based method for determining the most relevant training L-values is developed. These selected L-values serve as references to determine the likely quantization bin of unseen test data. This technique allows for a substantial decrease in the amount of memory required to store L-values per antenna symbol, an improvement of over 90% for a diverse range of scenarios. Following L-value quantization, a maximum likelihood detector is applied to retrieve the original data symbols. It was found that this approach results in a negligible performance loss, an increase in bit error rate (BER) threshold of no more than 0.3 dB for various modulation schemes and channel models. Simulation results comparing the technique to traditional, unsupervised methods are presented. Additionally, comparison experiments with conventional likelihood ratio quantization approaches that employ extensive training lists to determine the most similar training bins, known as best-matching training bins, revealed a 3.5 dB improvement in our method over this standard approach under certain conditions. Finally, a comparison experiment on our method and a state-of-the-art approach that also utilizes deep learning, called contrastive multi-view coding, revealed that our technique yields lower BER values for various scenarios. This research aims to contribute to the development of supervised quantization of L-values from likelihood ratios for gray-coded modulation schemes. It is our hope that these findings will facilitate the application of our technique to communication systems. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, while uncovering the first fixed-parameter results for parameterizations by treewidth and treedepth. We further demonstrate the applicability of our treedepth-based algorithm in solving an important problem in the field of consecutive k-colorings. Additionally, our treewidth-based algorithm yields a more efficient alternative to an earlier XP method for upward planarity, utilizing a linear number of planarity tests per vertex. Importantly, both new algorithms offer a significant reduction in computational complexity, particularly with respect to the number of recursive calls. Our treedepth-based algorithm performs better than the treewidth-based one, as it reduces the computational cost from $O(|T| \cdot c^w|$ to $O(|T| \cdot 2^{w/2})$. Our high-quality findings have been further verified using rigorous benchmarking tests to ensure their reliability and accuracy. The tests also highlighted the treedepth algorithm's superiority over the treewidth-based alternative. Furthermore, we've provided new insights on the complexity of the upward planarity problem by showing its PTIME solvability for k-outerplanar graphs and introducing a new graph class known as t-k-outerplanar, which facilitates a more refined graph classification in the realm of upward planarity. We've also conducted efficient solution times on various real-world network datasets. Finally, we've obtained an efficient planarity testing method for series-parallel graphs with bounded treedepth, which might be useful in independent research projects. We've also successfully applied our treedepth algorithm to the domain of linkages in the realm of upward planarity. The issue of efficiently identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout, with specific regard to the treedepth parameter, has been solved. Our high-quality findings have been thoroughly described and analyzed in the form of a detailed experimental analysis. For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which exhibit exponential decay in correlations, we can prove the exponential decay in the H\"older norm of the transfer operators acting on smooth observables. Importantly, this decay rate matches the correlation decay rate when the transfer operators' action is restricted to functions within a specified class. Additionally, for semiflows with lever-like behavior, we can extend this analysis to include decay in the decay rate itself, even in the presence of indifferent fixed points, thereby establishing exponential decay in the transfer operators' H\"older norm. This result holds not only for functions within any specific class but also across all functions of the same space, thus it significantly strengthens existing research in the field. Finally, to demonstrate the practical utility of these findings, we provide explicit estimates for the decay rate of the transfer operators acting on semiflows exhibiting mixing behavior, which is observed in the context of Lorentzian chaos. Furthermore, we showed that this analysis can be easily adapted to cover other models, such as piecewise affine maps and piecewise expanding maps with periodic induced maps, by conserving key properties. Moreover, we demonstrated that this theory's decay rate is closely related to the largest real part of the poles of the transfer operators' generating functions for these models. All the results mentioned were verified numerically to illustrate their accuracy. Last but not least, we explored the theoretical underpinning of our work, starting from the principles of dynamical systems theory, and systematically refined our arguments. This theoretical foundation will serve as a starting point for future enhancements to the paper's content. The supporting materials were compiled into an appendix. Thanks to all the suggestions and feedback we received, which ultimately led to considerable improvements to the paper's content. We examine EvoCrash's effectiveness and various optimizations, including the impact of time limits on mutations and the utility of guide code, to ensure accurate and efficient crash replication. We also discuss potential issues with EvoCrash's evaluations and provide suggestions for improving reliability and broadening its applicability. Our study centers on investigating the regular magnetic order (RMO) for certain spin models with global spin rotations symmetries, focusing on group theoretical methods for triangular and kagome lattices. These regular magnetic orders hold significance as potential ground states for various spin models, making them prime candidates for study. By adhering to a framework developed by Messio et al., we extended their initial approach to incorporate specific subgroupings of the p6m symmetry group, such as p6, p3, p3m1, and p31m. For kagome and triangular lattices fitting these groupings, we have identified all corresponding regular magnetic orders. Calculations were then performed to determine the energy and spin structure factors for each state examined. Furthermore, we have discussed the regular magnetic orders for a model involving nearest neighbor interactions on a triangular lattice, revealing a first order phase transition between the 120-degree and 90-degree ordered states. Our study also explores the regular magnetic orders for an edge-kagome lattice, illustrating a second order phase transition between the 120-degree and 60-degree ordered states. Lastly, we have developed initial findings on a rhombic kagome lattice featuring a p4 symmetry. All results were collected into comprehensive tables documenting 590 distinct regular magnetic orders across eight different groupings. The study's key results were presented in a conference report. Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal traits. To better grasp how people adapt to each other's communication style during conversations, it's necessary to analyze this adaptive synchronization, as it can reveal the underlying rules of interactions and relationships. This paper discusses the process of measuring adaptive synchronization through a deep analysis of conversational audio, focusing on the potential of using Affective-Net, a deep network model capable of identifying emotions, to detect the adaptation shifts, such as when emotions are expressed during interactions. Furthermore, it outlines the need for an unsupervised method to identify and categorize these adaptation moments in conversational speech more effectively. For this purpose, a new approach utilizing an unsupervised Hidden Markov Model combined with Deep Neural Networks is proposed, demonstrating its ability to identify normal and abnormal interaction patterns in audio samples. By incorporating this model, it is suggested that future research explore the link between emotional adaptation moments as an indicator of normal or abnormal interaction patterns, with the long-term goal of using entrainment as an early warning system for potential conflicts. This concept could revolutionize the fields of social psychology and clinical psychology by leveraging AI-powered analysis to identify relationship dynamics and potential for violent outbursts. Moreover, this model has the potential to be applied in other domains where understanding interaction patterns is crucial, such as marketing and computational propaganda studies. Unfortunately, the current dataset available for entrainment analysis is limited to recorded conversations between individuals with developmental disabilities and typical individuals, leaving a significant research gap to be explored in other areas of social psychology and artificial intelligence. Overall, this paper proposes a method to automatically identify normal and abnormal interaction patterns in conversational speech using Deep Neural Networks and other techniques. As part of the IEEE Technical Committee on Technical Achievement's (TCTA) activities, this research was supported by a grant in 2021, allowing the development of this innovative project. The resulting work has the potential to be applied in various domains, opening new avenues for research in the intersection of AI and social psychology. analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org). To create
these tools, we employed Quasar and Spectra, web-based frameworks formulated by
our team to facilitate interactive web-based visualizations for astronomical data
(https://quasar.g-array.org and https://spectra.g-array.org). In this work, we
detail the functionality of each tool, illustrate their capabilities through
rcSED2 dataset examples, and discuss potential applications for various astronomical
objects. The quasar.g-array.org and rcsed2.g-array.org websites provide access to
these tools, as well as demonstrating their integration with the rcSED2 catalog.

https://github.com/G-Array/rcsed2-visualizers. As an essential component of rcSED2,
these interactive visualizers facilitate comparison with astronomical objects
formerly or secretly known to humans (e.g., NGC 1068, NGC 4151), offering a
unified platform for seamlessly streaming, downloading, and exploring rcSED2's
spectra and imaging datasets, as well as uploading user-defined galaxy spectra
and imaging data for community analysis. Furthermore, the adoption of web-based
visualizers has significantly accelerated rcSED2's development, allowing the
dataset's expansion beyond initially anticipated bounds (comparing to rcSED first

creative ideas for analyzing and discussing astronomical phenomena, which may be

Classifying every video frame into its respective action can be a labor-intensive task, particularly for a large collection of unlabeled videos. Therefore, we present a novel, unsupervised method, called SSCAP, that identifies likely temporal segments across a variety of videos without the need for explicit annotations. SSCAP utilizes self-supervised learning techniques to distill semantic video segments that are universally applicable across a range of videos. By modeling the temporal relationships between frames in these segments, SSCAP accurately identifies the duration of each segment across a variety of videos. We validate the effectiveness of SSCAP through comprehensive experiments on two public datasets, while also evaluating its performance in combination with a strong baseline model, specifically spatial attention-based action parsing. We discover that the integration of SSCAP and action parsing results in substantial accuracy enhancements over existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate SSCAP's ability to generalize across different video content using two publicly available datasets while highlighting the detrimental effects of noisy temporal segments on segment accuracy. Finally, we illustrate the utility of SSCAP in application to multiple novel videos through an ablation study, revealing spatial coherence as a key factor in determining segment accuracy. SSCAP represents the first method to achieve competitive, state-of-the-art results on two public datasets without utilizing any explicit annotations. The method demonstrates significant potential for future advancement by bridging a major knowledge gap in the area of action segmentation without requiring any explicit annotations. The code for SSCAP has been made publicly available on this GitHub page.  Please feel free to contact us at kundu.saranya@gmail.com for further questions or comments on the content of this paper.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on chance rather than developing effective testing skills, as the emphasis is often superficial. To address this, we examined the perceptions of three university classes towards two different types of feedback: standard feedback highlighting uncovered parts of the code and intelligent feedback offering conceptual explanations for under-tested aspects. The goal was to compare these two approaches in terms of student understanding, program comprehension, and problem-solving abilities. The results indicated that using intelligent feedback led to higher levels of these skills for students who utilized it, as demonstrated by empirical data and statistical analysis. Furthermore, a follow-up investigation revealed that faculty using the intelligent feedback agent experienced an average increase of 25% in perceived utility, as much as 43% in reducing time spent on exam review, and a notable 33% decrease in time spent providing individual feedback. The study also identified several challenges associated with implementing conceptual feedback and offered recommendations for its effective deployment. The research suggested an opportunity to develop a more sophisticated agent that could automatically create conceptual under-standing materials for students, thus enhancing educational outcomes in software testing. The resulting prototype, known as FB-Spec, was developed, offering the foundation for a flexible and adaptable platform. The flexible nature of this prototype allowed for integrating it with existing tools used in professional settings, as the concept of using speculative testing to aid students in developing more effective test cases could be applied beyond traditional educational settings. The study's findings and results provide valuable insights for educators and researchers in the field of testing, while its impact extends to other disciplines where similar challenges related to testing methodologies and feedback mechanisms are present. To further investigate this, a companion study was conducted, examining the attitudes of professionals towards two distinct types of feedback: automatic and human-driven. The development of models for stellar, substellar, and planetary atmospheres heavily relies on accurate input data, specifically opacities, but various discrepancies often occur due to outdated or incomplete information about atomic and molecular interactions. In an attempt to bridge this gap, we compiled a comprehensive database of pre-calculated absorption coefficients for crucial atmospheric molecules such as MgH, SiO, TiO, and H2O, spanning a wide range of pressures, temperatures, and wavelengths. When necessary, we employed theoretical frameworks to account for the lack of available data, ensuring the broadest applicability possible. The effect of using different line lists was then evaluated within the context of Ultra-Hot Jupiters and M-dwarfs, where substantial differences were found in theoretical spectra and thermal profiles. Specifically, these discrepancies resulted in varying atmospheric scale heights, with variations in transmission spectra corresponding directly to the applied line lists. Consequently, the utilization of diverse line lists yields distinct results for their respective contributions to the thermal inversion, and differences this wide clearly impact the explanation of observed paucities in low-resolution spectra and the reported high abundances in high-resolution measurements. Ultimately, the utilization of our database is proposed for the generation of customized line lists for future missions, potentially leading to the optimization of model predictions based on prior assumptions and observations. The database, EXOPLINES, is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.737311. For the purposes of atmospheric modeling, a Python script is provided that facilitates the retrieval of molecular absorption coefficients for user-defined temperature, pressure, and wavelength inputs, as well as the analysis of synthetic spectra using degenerate matter and radiative transfer functions. This script can be accessed at https://github.com/AlyssaLester/exoplines. By addressing long-standing limitations of critical molecules, EXOPLINES positions itself as a vital resource for the simulation and analysis of substellar object atmospheres; however, recognition must also be given to various other line lists such as those of H2, whose contributions are not currently accounted for within our database. These quantum codes have the added benefit of having a substantial advantage in terms of decoding complexity compared to classical LDPC codes, with a significant performance gap increasing as the size of the code grows. The distance-$r$ dominating set problem, alongside its related covering problems, remains relatively unstudied within the framework of distributed computation for complex graph topologies. Unlike its more straightforward dominating set counterpart, a distributed algorithm is sought after for solving the $r$-distance dominating set problem, which poses challenges due to the lack of a polylogarithmic solution in certain sparse graph types, such as for a limited degree of $O(\log^r n)$, even in simpler product graph models. However, for a more restricted class of graphs known as high-girth bipartite, a precise logarithmic upper bound of $O(\log n)$ is shown to be achievable in a more restricted setting of just five or more 'girths of separation'. Furthermore, for our developed algorithm to function in bipartite graphs of $O(\log^c n)$ degree (where $c < 1.5$) with additional requirements, such as a known polynomial upper bound on the number of colors needed for a proper vertex coloring, then this algorithm will succeed in producing a distance-$r$ dominating set in bipartite graphs of girth at least five. In particular, for the specific instance where $r = 3$, then a polynomial time solution is shown to be achievable in bipartite graphs of girth at least six, thereby achieving a better result than previously known distributed algorithms for the more generally defined 3-distance dominating set problem. Lastly, a set of bipartite graph properties, known as 'bipartite $q$-factor', encompassing girth, is identified and in particular, for the specific instance where $r = 3$, then a set of 'easy' bipartite $3$-factor graphs is identified in which the $r$-distance dominating set problem can be solved in a polynomial time solution, notably including the well known M\"{u}ller's graphs of degree $\log n$ and the randomized variants of the ratio of the number of colors needed for a proper vertex coloring over the girth of the graph $g$. This research examines the impact of disorder on the correlation between bulk and boundaries in two-dimensional topological insulators of higher order. We explore two specific scenarios: one focusing on the relationship between boundary zero modes and bulk states in the presence of time reversal symmetry, and the other examining the correlation between boundary states with non-zero Hall conductivities when time reversal symmetry is breached. For the first scenario, we establish that bulk states can give rise to multiple boundary zero modes, and introduce a method to count these zero modes reliably. We also develop a set of rules that enable us to determine the precise number of bulk-boundary correspondence pairs under disorder for boundary states with non-zero Hall conductivities. Our findings indicate that disorder does not completely break the bulk-boundary correspondence, but rather enables various forms of correspondence between bulk and boundary states. We illustrate the applicability of our rules via examples of Kondo boxes and HgTe bilayers under disorder. For the second scenario, we establish that boundary states with non-zero Hall conductivities can serve as an effective means of implementing a bulk-boundary correspondence. We also determine the precise numbers of boundary states with non-zero Hall conductancies that can participate in the bulk-boundary correspondence in various disordered systems, including HgTe bilayers, Kondo boxes, and Bi$_3$Pe$_2$Ge$_2$O$_{11}$. Finally, we outline a strategy for identifying and experimenting on topological insulators of higher order in which the bulk-boundary correspondence is purely implemented by zero-energy boundary modes. Our research demonstrates the crucial role that disorder and symmetry considerations play in establishing the bulk-boundary correspondence in the study of topological insulators of higher order. Additionally, we provide new insights into the characteristics of disordered systems that exhibit unique properties under both time reversal and charge conservation. Such insights pave the way for future theoretical and experimental investigations of topological insulators of higher order in the presence of disorder. The research is implemented within the QuantumDot package, a comprehensive tool for investigating the characteristics of zero-dimensional systems under both time reversal and charge conservation. As a result, our research demonstrates the crucial influence that disorder and symmetry considerations have on the bulk-boundary correspondence in the study of topological insulators of higher order, and inspires future research into the wide variety of topological insulators of higher order in the presence of disorder. Recent searches for supersymmetry at the classical level have not provided any conclusive signs of new physics. In response, the CMS is implementing specialized searches aimed at more complex and precise supersymmetry scenarios. This contribution will focus on three new searches using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data recorded with the CMS detector between 2016 and 2018: a heavy gluino search involving the decay of heavy neutralinos and resulting in boosted Z bosons and undetected energy; a search for supersymmetry compression in final states featuring soft tau particles; and an investigation into compressed, long-lived charginos in hadronic final states displaying vanished particle tracks. Each of these novel searches seeks to address limitations of existing CMS analyses by targeting supersymmetry scenarios not previously explored. Furthermore, these new searches aim to enhance the coverage of SUSY compression scenarios, a phenomenon characteristic of numerous theoretical models. In addition to these new searches, the CMS is implementing compressed and long-lived scenarios within two existing searches as additional validation tests. These new searches will significantly expand the range of SUSY parameters that can be probed, substantially lowering the allowable mass of gluinos and long-lived particles to be in line with theoretical predictions. Consequently, these new searches will significantly boost the likelihood of detecting supersymmetry at 95% confidence level, increasing it by factors of almost 20 and 8 respectively, and broadening the range of SUSY mass splittings in which supersymmetry can be detected at statistical significance. Assuming a simplified theoretical model, the CMS is capable of probing SUSY at mass levels far beyond the existing upper limits of 2 and 3 TeV set by the LHC searches for heavy, long-lived particles in 2017 and 2018 respectively. In summary, these novel searches represent important enhancements to the CMS supersymmetry search programme, effectively expanding the range of Supersymmetry parameters into the multi-TeV regime. Assuming a simplified theoretical model, the CMS is capable of probing mass levels up to 5-20 TeV, and the detection of Supersymmetry will significantly increase with these new searches at mass levels spanning from 1-3, 3-5 and 5-20 TeV, and at 95% confidence level respectively. Novel view synthesis with light field rendering traditionally achieves accurate reproduction of view-dependent phenomena by densely sampling a scene's views, yet these processes are often computationally expensive. In contrast, geometric reconstruction methods only require sparse views but often struggle to replicate non-Lambertian light interactions. Our new model strikes a balance by learning view-dependent effects in four-dimensional light field space and inferring scene geometry using sparse views and geometric constraints. Specifically, we developed a two-stage transformer architecture that combines epipolar and reference view aggregations to compute target ray colors, demonstrating superior performance over existing techniques across multiple benchmark datasets, particularly in scenes with pronounced view-dependent changes. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on newly recorded datasets capturing prominent view-dependent effects from frozen waterfall scenes and soft lighting scenarios. Our code is available at:  https://github.com/stтех/light-field-neural-rendering.  The corresponding video is at:  https://youtu.be/fxkxkW5loU8.  The video demonstrates the importance of accurate scene geometry and view-dependent effects for realistic novel view synthesis.  For additional information, please visit our project website at:  https://michaelassibity.github.com/light-field-neural-rendering/. A powerful and dynamic solar eruption triggered by shock waves emanating from the Sun's corona can accelerate electrons, resulting in the formation of type II radio bursts. Although these bursts have been observed extensively, researchers continue to investigate their origin. To address this, we studied a notable solar eruption on October 16, 2015, that involved an EUV jet, a streamer in white-light, and a type II radio burst observed in the low frequency range. By analyzing these separate manifestations of the event, we established that the source of the type II radio burst and the extended streamer coincided and moved at the same speed. We discovered that the episode of enhanced radio emission corresponding to the streamer was lacking in the high frequency component typically associated with shock accelerated electrons. Furthermore, using the 2015 event in conjunction with similar observations from 2013, we found that these bursts often occur near the solar equator, particularly during the maximum of the solar cycle. By taking into consideration the spatial extent, frequency, and duration of these radio bursts, we found they generally require a more substantial energy input than that provided by small-scale solar jets. Instead, these bursts are more likely triggered by the driving of piston shocks through large equatorial streamers by the motion of coronal structures hosting flares or other forms of energy release from the coronal plane. This greater insight into the underlying process allows us to reevaluate the traditional low frequency type II burst generation mechanism as generally applicable only in the equatorial regions near solar maxima. It is there that increased activity and reconnection due to shearing motions in magnetic loops likely create conditions allowing for the propagation of MHD shocks along magnetic field lines to drive the formation and propagation of MHD piston shocks in the corona, capable of accelerating electrons at these low frequencies. It is also there that these shock accelerated electrons retain sufficient energy to give rise to the high frequency radio bursts typically observed in type II solar eclipsences. However, this new mechanism is inherently applicable only in the equatorial regions, requiring a specific magnetic configuration, generally unavailable at higher latitudes, which generally corresponds to decreased solar activity levels. Consequently, it is there that these bursts are more frequently observed in the maximum of the solar cycle. A detailed likelihood analysis is performed on the general two Higgs doublet model in order to investigate its capacity to address the anomalies observed in $b\to c$ transitions, as well as the observed deviation in the muon's magnetic moment from standard model predictions. The model's parameter space is explored under both its tree-level and loop-level effects on the mentioned phenomena. The results show that although the model is capable of effectively resolve some of the anomalies observed in $b\to c$ transitions, it fails to address the observed deviation in the muon's magnetic moment after incorporating the latest CMS data. Additionally, this model is shown to provide a poorer fit to the combined Bu->cl+u- data when compared to the single channel results. Considering the various systematic effects that could affect these findings, this analysis still concludes that the model's capacity to address all observed anomalies remains challenging. Furthermore, this analysis draws a parallel between the world data on $b\to s\mu+\mu-$ transitions and the muon's magnetic moment anomaly, similar to recent two Higgs doublet model studies examining the former. Ultimately, this analysis highlights the need for continued Muon g-2 and LHCb measurements in the coming years, which are expected to have significant implications for two Higgs doublet model parameter space and double Higgs production observations at the Large Hadron Collider. These future findings will likely offer a more conclusive understanding of two Higgs doublet model parameters and potentially validate the observed anomalies within this theoretical framework. Furthermore, this analysis is easily adaptable to other models addressing these anomalies and can be expanded to investigate double Higgs production and other phenomenological signatures. This study introduces a unique, self-contained three-dimensional random vortex system that mirrors the behavior of the Navier-Stokes equations for non-viscous incompressible fluid flows. The state vector of a boson sampling process can be precisely generated using S single photons passed through beam splitters with M modes, facilitating a study of its entanglement. Measuring entanglement in multipartite systems, however, poses significant challenges due to the vast dimension of the boson sampling process's Hilbert space, particularly for large values of S and M. Consequently, previous analyses were restricted to smaller systems, such as S=4 and M=2,3, where certain aspects of entanglement were explored, but not all relevant parameters. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new set of observables, called W, that enables a comprehensive comprehension of the boson sampling state's entanglement across various criteria, including purity, entanglement of formation, and specific measures like spin-symmetry and mode-dependent entanglement. Moreover, these observables allow for the simulation of entanglement in systems exceeding the physical limitations of experimental setups, such as S=5 and M=4, thereby significantly expanding our knowledge of entanglement in boson sampling processes. By combining numerical simulations with experimental data collected from a 3S, 4-mode setup, this paper establishes a clear distinction between measurements based on our proposed method and those of other multiparticle observables like Bell-like random, Greenberg, and Peres-Mermin. The introduced approach empowers researchers to investigate novel properties of entanglement in boson sampling state vectors and to distinguish it from the effects produced by non-local correlations, which can be achieved with fewer, properly engineered qubits compared to the boson sampling process. Specifically, this paper demonstrates that boson sampling states exhibit unique properties of spin-symmetry, mode-dependent entanglement, and specific measures like EoF when measured with W, and shows that these entanglement properties significantly differ from the effects produced by Bell-like correlations, which are found in a certain quantum system with 4 qubits. Consequently, this paper enables a comprehensive analysis of the boson sampling state's entanglement across all its parameters through numerical simulations, thereby advancing our understanding of entanglement in quantum systems beyond the limitations of Bell-like correlations. Lastly, future research possibilities are outlined. Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression difference or correlation measures that are unreliable for supervised learning. As a result, vital insights into diseases and biological processes are yet to be uncovered. We introduce TELOS, a novel, efficient, and accurate method for analyzing temporal sequence data in a supervised context. We compare the effectiveness of TELOS with traditional approaches like MATISO and Time-Warped Dynamic Time Warping (TW-DTW), demonstrating its superiority through in-depth simulations and real-world applications. While our comparisons show that TW-DTW outperforms other methods, the methods based on time-warping are computationally inefficient. We also showcase TELOS's efficacy in understanding stages of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy from blood samples using a Microarray-KNN-SVM hybrid model. TELOS offers a range of powerful and efficient measures that are applicable to various statistical models and algorithms. We provide access to our source code through a GitHub repository. Overall, the effectiveness of TELOS in analyzing temporal sequence data holds promising potential for transforming supervised learning in the life sciences sector. We conduct an additional study exploring the use of TELOS for analyzing COVID-19 symptoms and biomarkers in a real-world medical setting. Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the highest achieving strategies through interactions with complex systems, even when the underlying rules are unknown. Many successful methods utilize a valuation function to estimate the most beneficial course of action at any given point, but this approach can become extremely challenging in partially observable settings. Partially observable environments are characterized by a lack of complete information about the overall state, leading to a notable increase in the complexity of the decision-making process. One technique for addressing these situations involves the use of recurrent neural networks, which can learn to approximate an expanded state that takes into account prior behavior and perceived observations, thereby facilitating more informed decision-making. Notably, this learned representation shares a resemblance to the concept of belief state found in theoretical models. However, the relationship between these concepts remains largely unexplored. To shed light on this topic, we seek to bridge the theoretical divide between partially observable reinforcement learning and the fast-moving field of deep reinforcement learning, particularly as it concerns the application of neural networks to the estimation of a putative belief state. To illustrate this point, we draw on a case study involving a real-world robot motion control problem that requires navigating a dynamic environment. This investigation involves a rigorous analysis of a theoretical model known as the partially observable reinforcement learning algorithm, as well as an empirical comparison between this model and a corresponding algorithm grounded in deep learning. By demonstrating that deep-learning-based estimates of the belief state closely align with the outcomes of the theoretical model, we establish a concrete empirical link between these previously disjoint ideas. Furthermore, we show that these estimates can serve as a valuable surrogate for the actual belief state and aid in more accurate prediction and better decision-making. Ultimately, this finding highlights the potential for neural networks to facilitate a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between agents, environments, and state in partially observable settings. As such, this work marks an effort to integrate theoretical and empirical approaches to partially observable reinforcement learning, thereby fostering greater collaboration and knowledge exchange between these fields. Notably, while our investigation focuses on the application of recurrent networks, we contend that similar techniques hold the potential for improving decision-making in a broad range of partially observable situations. To that end, we include an additional empirical case study involving a classic testing ground known as the "roller coaster," which underscores the significance of contextual influences in shaping the effectiveness of partially observable policies. Following the recommended guidelines, we present our findings in the form of a paper, including accompanying videos. A version of this work was initially presented at the IJCAI Conference in 2017.

In video action detection, current research faces two significant limitations. Firstly, the dependency on heavily annotated bounding boxes in every video complicates scalability and reproducibility. Secondly, the conventional method of training strong classifiers using dense proposals for top-performing performance is computationally expensive and impractical. This results in suboptimal performance and high processing requirements. To overcome these challenges, we have devised a novel framework called Spot. Spot is built on two powerful ideas. Firstly, it utilizes a unique program for automatically spotting actions within proposals based on the whole-body context of the video. This allows it to effectively combine handcrafted and deep body part features to determine the importance of each proposal. Secondly, it employs a hybrid model to integrate spatial and temporal context from multiple proposal features for precise action detection. This is achieved through the use of Graph Convolutional Networks, eliminating the need for pre-trained box-based features. Experimental evaluations on benchmarks such as ActivityNet and VL-KITTI have shown that Spot surpasses state-of-the-art performance while maintaining scalability and efficiency. For instance, it achieves a 43.9 mAP on ActivityNet at 14 fsymbols per frame on a single GPU, outperforming the current best method by 12.7 points. Code for Spot is accessible on the repository at https://github.com/zhang9208/Spot.00. This repository contains the code for Spot.00.

With over 200 participants involved, the winning entries are subjected to both qualitative and quantitative analysis in this paper. Key findings indicate that the most challenging transformations for the participating algorithms are extreme cropping of images, incorporation into unrelated content, combined with pixel-level disturbances. Notably, the winning approaches employed training with robustly augmented data, self-supervised learning methods, score normalization techniques, explicit identification of overlays, and pair-wise image comparison utilizing global descriptors. Furthermore, the analysis revealed several intriguing patterns in the dataset's nature. Ultimately, the findings and outcomes of the challenge provide valuable insights for advancing copy scene detection research. Our research involves analyzing stochastic processes that are either halted or move along the boundary of a given domain, and we study how these processes are affected by specific equations from the parabolic family under various assumptions. These equations may experience degeneration, which means their stochastic operators' lower eigenvalues change between positive and non-positive values as parameters shift. Our investigation centers on how these processes behave when these equations undergo various types of perturbations, and how this impact influences the stochastic processes' metastability. This study also addresses the problem of stabilizing or preventing stochastic processes from reaching their goal by using therapy and includes a demonstration of these principles in a model surrounding biological cell movements. Additionally, we explore the principles of homogenization, which allows us to understand the long-term behavior of these stochastic processes, and how this process can be applied to a specific model of surface growth. Our work is based on three main types of problems: problems with gradual changes, problems with sudden changes, and problems with periodic changes, each characterized by the nature of these perturbations. Finally, we outline future research directions related to these problems. Our findings indicate that high magnetic fields have a substantial impact on the structure and energy of matter composed of neutrons and protons, and that this effect increases with the strength of the magnetic field. Moreover, our analysis of the saturation properties of nuclear matter in high-field conditions reveals that application of the LLOCV technique is essential for obtaining accurate results. Additionally, our model suggests that, at a moderate magnetic field of around 5 billion Gauss, the ratio of neutrons to protons is roughly 1.8. Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this gap, we have created an innovative approach that reconciles the requirements of efficient communication and differential privacy. We integrated Relative Entropy Coding, a highly efficient compression technique, into the distributed training framework. By introducing a simple adjustment to REC, we derived a differential privacy compliant algorithm, which provides quantifiable guarantees. Experimental results show that our approach substantially decreases communication costs while maintaining high data privacy standards. Notably, DP-REC achieved a 5.95x reduction in transmission volume over vanilla REC at a minimal precision loss of 0.01%. Furthermore, our approach maintains competitive classification accuracy with the baseline REC model, with a loss of just 0.35%. Finally, we found that our approach meets its desired goal of achieving a reliable trade-off between communication efficiency and data privacy. The resource-intensive process of rigorous experimentation was made more efficient via the utilization of cloud resources. By cloud optimization, we could train the neural network 2.25 times faster. We validate the effectiveness of the approach through rigorous experimentation. Structured tables in various documents effectively present complex information, making research in scientific papers easily accessible to scholars by compiling experimental outcomes and highlighting novel discoveries. Current table analysis techniques can fall short due to recognition errors stemming from the conversion of PDFs into document images, resulting in information loss. This study develops a solution to table extraction by leveraging Graph Neural Networks and incorporates tailored representation embeddings that improve differentiation between tables, table headers, and other document elements. An experimental assessment was conducted on a combined dataset from PubLayNet and PubTables-1M to validate the efficacy of the proposed method. The findings demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a high F1-score of 0.838 for accurate table detection in a diverse range of documents. Furthermore, the underlying solution has been made available through a GitHub repository for widespread use. An additional benefit of the publication includes an in-depth analysis of the representation's impact and a novel dataset composed of PubLayNet's visual table representations, which serves as a valuable resource for the scientific community. The paper's further visibility is enhanced via showcases on YouTube.  The F1-score of the table recognition models was achieved through the combination of the developed representation module and a Graph Neural Networks-based table extraction model. An accurate understanding of the table and its contents were obtained by applying the Mediovilian Graph Neural Networks to the extracted table. The architecture utilizes an ensemble of three different models to improve its overall performance by switching between different graph nodes during training. This technique allows the model to sample and combine the predictions of the three different models, which enhances the final output. By using the developed technique, the table extraction model was able to achieve a F1-score of 0.838, while demonstrating a significant improvement of 0.154 compared to the baseline dataset provided by PubLayNet. The table extraction model was implemented using the Pytorch framework, which offers a flexible and powerful environment for building machine learning models. In addition to the code used to develop the solution, the repository includes the necessary code to train, test, and evaluate the model. This code can serve as a starting point for researchers and practitioners looking to develop similar solutions, which ultimately aims to enhance the quality of the table analysis. The repository contains the solution and the underlying code was made available under the MIT license, which allows for easy adoption and modification by other researchers. The modified version of the dataset was published under a joint CC0 license, which simplifies its reuse and sharing among the community. This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, introducing a new model that evolves over multiple rounds of incomplete information games. Each player is initially assumed to be a simple Bayesian evaluator, with the possibility of being upgraded to a more sophisticated state-action estimator as they accumulate more experience with their opponent's strategy. We investigate how this dynamic cognitive hierarchy affects player behavior in two-seat auctions with a high bidding cost, showing that it aligns with experimental findings. Furthermore, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the new model's properties using a range of incomplete information games, revealing key insights into the underlying dynamics. We demonstrate that smaller cognitive hierarchy types result in slower cognitive growth, whereas larger types may lead to incomplete information equilibrium outcomes. We also show that varying the size of the cognitive hierarchy can introduce instability under certain conditions. Lastly, we utilize the dynamic cognitive hierarchy to examine equilibrium outcomes in two-stage auctions where intermediaries hold information advantage, showing that it yields higher revenues for intermediates compared to the simple Bayesian cognitive hierarchy model. We verify these results through a direct comparison with the static cognitive hierarchy model. We believe that this research significantly contributes to the theory of dynamic cognitive hierarchy, and with the introduction of the new model, it becomes feasible for future studies to explore a broader range of applications. We performed a comprehensive comparative analysis of the new model's equilibrium outcomes across various cognitive hierarchy types, providing key insights into the underlying dynamics. We show that the dynamic cognitive hierarchy is a stable system, supporting the notion that larger types prefer simpler types, and that taller types tend to grow faster. We also conduct a detailed analysis of the properties of the new model using a range of incomplete information games, and show that it can lead to equilibrium outcomes that are both symmetric and asymmetric under specific conditions. We identify an interesting paradox in the dynamic cognitive hierarchy setting, showing that an infinite increase in the type of a simple Bayesian player may eventually result in a lower revenue for an intermediary relative to the simplest type. We demonstrate that this paradox highlights an important requirement for the size of the cognitive hierarchy, stating that a larger size should yield a higher revenue for an intermediary. We also show that the dynamic cognitive hierarchy is a consistent model that can result in a higher revenue for intermediates compared to the simple Bayesian cognitive hierarchy model. Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As censuses fall short of meeting these needs, Demographic Estimation Techniques (DETs) offer an alternative solution. We evaluated the effectiveness of the back-projection method in predicting Mozambique's population trends between 2000 and 2015, utilizing weekly infant mortality rate data from 2006 to 2015 and adjusting for vaccination progress. Our analysis revealed significant discrepancies between estimated and actual population figures at ten-year census intervals. While corrections for vaccination had minimal impact on these disparities, we discovered that errors in the calculation of graduate rates significantly influenced the accuracy of population estimates. These findings highlight the importance of using accurate graduate distribution coefficients to produce reliable population estimates. As such, we propose a framework for enhancing the estimation process by incorporating latest census data and fine-tuning the model with additional years of data. Our research signifies the first step in developing a sustainable population estimation model for Mozambique, one that can operate independently from censuses. Furthermore, our proposed framework has the potential to be applied in other countries, particularly those with comparable data availability. The next stage of our research will involve refining the model for short-term forecasting, a capability that would enable us to generate more accurate and timely estimates for policymakers. By achieving this goal, we will ultimately contribute to a better understanding of population dynamics in Mozambique, enabling the effective planning of resources within the country. As the need for continuous population estimation is increasing globally, we will make a significant contribution to the development of a sustainable estimation model in several countries, starting with Mozambique. The model code and data will be made publicly available through our GitHub repository. The model's predictive abilities will be assessed through a short-term forecasting exercise following the framework proposed by Williams et al. The outcome of this exercise, which is currently in progress, will be shared as a separate preprint. Over the past ten years, substantial advancements have taken place to minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems. These developments led to the creation of novel systems such as cuckoo and xor filters. Moreover, meta-algorithms were introduced that combine multiple filters in the form of an ensemble. Ensembles were shown to effectively decrease the likelihood of incorrect positive results, achieving rates five times lower than traditional solutions. However, meta-algorithms introduce an additional complication: it becomes more challenging to determine with certainty if a query is part of a particular set. This paper presents a new type of ensemble-based filter designed to eliminate incorrect positive results regarding membership queries. The proposed filter requires significant advancements in the design of its building blocks as well as a novel approach to combining the results of individual filters. Experimental findings demonstrate that the proposed ensemble-based filter allows us to determine with certainty if a query is part of a particular set (i.e., true negative results are provided without delay), accomplishes this task four times more efficiently than current solutions, and preserves a constant efficiency compared to existing ones when answering queries about set membership. Moreover, the proposed filter preserves the ability to retrieve information about set membership at no additional cost. Finally, experimental results indicate that the proposed filter achieves a four-fold reduction in the likelihood of incorrect positive results compared to current solutions, maintaining a constant incorrect positive results rate when answering queries about set membership. Compared to existing ensemble-based filters, the proposed filter preserves their efficiency in determining with certainty if a query is part of a particular set (i.e., true negative results are provided without delay), while reducing the additional overhead imposed by the likelihood of incorrect positive results by a factor of three. This paper is available under the terms of the open-source license, allowing to reduce the likelihood of incorrect positive results. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay of superpositions of one atom and one molecule coexist with stable two-spin atom-molecule pairs. The relative weight of these superpositions can be manipulated by adjusting the intensity of a radio frequency field. Our research also demonstrates that the mixing of spin states via a radio frequency field, under specific vanishing Rabi frequencies, does not result in molecule production. Furthermore, we employed a two-state clock model to investigate the interplay of states with differing parities during atom-molecule conversion and found that this leads to a reduction in stability of the two-spin atom-molecule pair as clock states become increasingly misaligned. Our study of scenarios with negligible two-body interaction during atom-molecule conversion reveals the emergence of a long-lived clock-like instability at specific dark-state conditions, resulting in oscillating atom-molecule pairs and their associated spins. In cases where a significant two-body interaction is present, we identified an equilibrium point of these oscillations and provided an expression to calculate a related "coupling constant." The derived coupling constant can potentially facilitate the creation of stable two-spin atom-molecule pairs through a process known as spin dynamics. The study also explores the general conditions under which light-induced atom-molecule conversion fails, citing recent experimental findings as an example of this phenomenon where the resulting atom-molecule pair experiences a lossy dynamics. Lastly, we have shown that the mean field approach does not accurately describe the results of a specific light-induced atom-molecule conversion experiment, even when the resulting atom-molecule pair has a low relative weight of a one-atom and one-molecule superposition. The relevant light-induced one-spin-atom-molecule transformation experiments are noted in the last section of this study. The study is conducted with a goal of informing and interpreting recent atom-molecule conversion experiments. In other words, it can't control pitch well beyond a certain range.  We suggest two new algorithms to fix this issue.  First, we came up with a pitch-shifting method that doesn't change a model's idea of how speech sounds.  We then used this idea in a new, larger set of speech samples that are pitched higher or lower than normal.  We tested several ways to do pitch augmentation and picked the one that gave the best results.  We also came up with a simple way to gradually change the pitch values in a sentence.  Our results show that these techniques are very helpful in making more natural changes to the pitch of the speech samples.  We also found that using the pitch augmentation in a natural-sounding way yields a significant 35% better speech quality score in a model that controls pitch well, and a 23% better score in a model that doesn't, compared to not using the augmentation at all. This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based reasoning challenges in videos by employing object persistence principles. A crucial element of our strategy is to carefully design the graph for representing relationships between objects across different frames. In this study, we introduce Hopper, a model based on transformers that can follow objects' movements multi-step ahead, allowing us to build a strong baseline for spatiotemporal reasoning. By utilizing 1D spatial self-attention layers to encode object features, we can represent and store these features effectively. Additionally, we propose using an enhanced graph construction method that significantly reduces the need for manually labeled data during the training process. Our enhanced graph strategy begins by identifying pairs of objects that remain the same throughout the video and also applies to challenging scenarios where multiple steps are involved. Furthermore, we are one of the few studies that tackle multi-hop challenges where we achieve a new state-of-the-art performance on both existing and introduced benchmark datasets. This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the oriented colored broken submersions b-principle to the Kaehler-Einstein program for complex projective planes. Furthermore, it highlights how this b-principle could offer an innovative perspective on prioritizing the order of exploring outcomes in the study of Madsen-Weiss theorem and its underlying components. A detailed comparison between the oriented colored broken submersions b-principle and miller-mumford paradigm is also provided at the end of the note. Our work is a natural extension of Miller's and that of Muntean\^o-Weinberg's recent findings.

The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from past experiences like humans. This capability is referred to as knowledge transferability. Typically, the process of DTL begins by initially training DNNs on general knowledge and then utilizing them for specific tasks through a refinement process called fine-tuning. There have been two commonly observed patterns of transferability among pre-trained DNNs: one being that larger gaps between pre-training data and downstream information result in lower transferability and another indicating that transferability tends to decline from the initial to the final stages of a DNN. Nevertheless, these findings were primarily based on a limited range of datasets and only considered the performance of a DNN after fine-tuning the last weight layers. This research aims to improve upon existing consensus through a comprehensive collection of diverse natural image datasets that are representative of unique downstream tasks. This research demonstrates that there are two commonly observed trends of transferability among pre-trained DNNs: one suggesting that downstream information with higher visual complexities requires pre-training data with lower complexities to yield lower transferability and another indicating that transferability tends to decline from non-linear to linear feature learning stages of a DNN. This research also demonstrates that there are two commonly observed trends of transferability among pre-trained DNNs: one suggesting that transferability tends to decline from head to tail of a DNN and another indicating that transferability tends to decline from initial to final feature learning stages of a DNN. This research also demonstrates the effectiveness of utilizing partial DNNs to alleviate the challenges of DNNs during initialization and to save computation costs during fine-tuning process.
