Following Quantum Chromodynamics' 1972 formulation, a breakthrough in its regularization came when Kenneth Wilson applied it to Euclidean lattices. This opened the door to a range of theoretical advancements in the field, which I will outline in this talk, particularly focusing on the seminal contributions made in the early years of lattice QCD studies. Key progress in the field, related to finite temperature and density QCD studies, will be discussed along with the consequential impact on the investigation of QCD's phase transitions. Furthermore, I will provide an overview of the current status of lattice QCD studies aimed at understanding the phase transitions between the various low-energy states of QCD that may exist at its phase boundaries with a range of potential phase transitions being investigated.  These states, which include a crystalline state known as quark matter and the possibility of deconfinement and chiral condensation transitions, will be discussed along with the use of lattice QCD to investigate the phase transitions that may separate these distinct states of QCD.  While lattice QCD is currently the only reliable theoretical tool to investigate QCD's phase transitions, it is limited in its ability to handle realistic conditions, particularly when it comes to pressure, chemical potential and the curvature of its equation of state. Therefore, a range of theoretical tools, some of which are discussed in this talk, are exploring QCD's equation of state in order to investigate these limitations of lattice QCD and the realism of its predictions for its equation of state.  These predictions will be discussed in relation to the various low-energy states of QCD that may exist.  In addition to these discussions of QCD's phase transitions, I will also overview the currently most advanced theoretical model being used to investigate QCD's equation of state, which is based on the 3-dimensional Ising model. This talk will provide an in-depth overview into the development of this model being applied to the 4-dimensional QCD and the reliance of this model's equations on the symmetries that are responsible for QCD's phase transitions.  These symmetries will be discussed in some depth along with the role of the renormalisation group in investigating QCD's phase transitions.  In addition to these discussions of the physics of QCD's phase transitions, I will also be able to provide some insights into the current debate as to the possible role of topological features in QCD's phase transitions and the current debate as to the possible role of the renormalisation group in investigating QCD's phase transitions. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this study, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and explicitly calculate the lower central series for $\Gamma_n$. Additionally, $\Gamma_n$ is defined as the semidirect product of a copy of $\mathbb{Z}$ with a free group of rank $n-1$, subject to a specific action. Notably, our research shows that $\Gamma_n$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property for all $n\geq 2$. Further investigation involved finding the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degrees for various generalized versions of the Baumslagt-Solitar groups, specifically GSBS$_m$ obtained from $\Gamma_n$ but with the $\mathbb{Z}$ action multiplied by $m$. In this instance, our research indicates that GSBS$_1$ is isomorphic to the group $\psi_n(G)$. Moreover, our results yield that GSBS$_1$ is isomorphic to $\psi_n(G)$ possess the $R_\infty$ property. 20 to 40 minutes. Our primary aim in creating this dataset is to supply the

trajectories, driving speeds, and locations on the road. By utilizing the
NDDTool, we extracted 43,617 scenarios from the SceNDD dataset. To facilitate

We are investigating a type of equality related to the work exerted on a system being observed with unsharp, non-projective measurement methods. We establish work by comparing the final expected energy level with the energy measurement result $f$, which has been obtained and the subsequent expectation value. The proof involves the introduction of a new type of equality, the single measurement result Integral Fluctuation Equality (SRIFE), for $\langle E(f)\rangle$, valid for any measurement. For ideal projective measurements, the usual integral Fluctuation Equality (IFE) applies. We derive the IFE and SRIFE for a specific type of quantum map, the rotator, to demonstrate their distinct nature. Furthermore, we use the SRIFE to derive a new inequality for arbitrary quantum processes. We then consider experiments that are not dependent on the outcome, or post-selecting, to understand the influence of the measurement in these scenarios. Finally, for ideal measurements, the SRIFE is related to the Jarzynski Equality (JE) by means of a conditional average. Consequently, the JE can be derived from the SRIFE. However, the SRIFE can be derived from the IFE, indicating that the SRIFE is more general than previously thought. We then derive the SRIFE for specific types of quantum dynamics: for conserving quantum systems with mixed measurements, a new equality related to the dynamical work is introduced, analogous to the IFE. We also derive the SRIFE for non-interacting particle conserving quantum dynamics. Furthermore, we use perturbation theory to apply the SRIFE to a quantum harmonic oscillator for both general and ideal measurements in a systematic expansion. We then consider a fundamental issue of emergent thermodynamics, namely how a distance based inequality for dynamic work, the emergent thermodynamic work inequality (ETWI), relates to measurable work. We achieve this goal by deriving the ETWI from measurable work based on the SRIFE obtained for quantum dynamics. However, an additional assumption is required to obtain a more tight lower bound then was previously known. We use an exact analytical calculation for a rotator to confirm the tightness of the new lower bound then known. We apply a belief that the measurable dynamic work is thought to be the work exerted by the system being observed with unsharp, non-projective measurement methods. As part of the effort to combat this crisis, contact tracing technology, known for its success in other outbreaks, has been widely adopted.  However, implementing contact tracing technology on a large scale raises significant concerns regarding user privacy, leading to hesitation among some users to adopt these services. A security framework called Coronav'SUS is introduced, which provides a reliable foundation for future research.  While the proposed approach offers better privacy protection than existing COVID-19 contact tracing apps, it still poses some security risks, mainly due to the use of GPS location tracking, which can compromise user privacy, leading to the creation of a setting to control GPS data collection for COVID-19 Exposures. This setting controls the submission of GPS data to the health authorities, ensuring that users can choose what information to share, while the Coronav'SUS framework maintains the Exposures submitted by users to the health authorities. Although the proposed approach reduces privacy concerns, it still relies on the integrity of health authorities to handle user data anonymously and ensure the confidentiality of submissions. The central nervous system's underlying physiological processes that drive conscious experiences have long been a puzzle in understanding human consciousness. In physiological terms, this puzzle revolves around the role of blood flow and neural activity, with the latter being electrical impulses between neurons. Despite ongoing discussions, there is still significant uncertainty surrounding the consciousness-emerging properties of these neural networks. This essay explores recent advancements in understanding the physical mechanisms behind consciousness, with a primary focus on one of the leading theories - Integrated Information Theory (IIT). This theory postulates that consciousness arises from a universal mechanism involving information integration within and among neural systems. While IIT offers a mechanistic framework for understanding the underlying processes, it relies heavily on a type of physical process known as integration information. This essay argues that IIT is best interpreted through a more fine-grained, quantum theoretical framework, incorporating two of the three IIT principles, with the third being generated through a more refined analysis. This refined analysis requires a more intricate notion of integration, one that surpasses the current classical and quantum technical capabilities. Nonetheless, this more refined notion can be employed to demonstrate a conceptual link between IIT and a similar neural theory (the Global Workspace Theory), as well as addressing the long-standing debate between local and global integration, with the latter suggesting that local integrations can collectively produce global integrations. Ultimately, this more refined notion may facilitate a deeper grasp of the underlying processes behind human consciousness. One potential implementation of this refined notion is illustrated through a case study in beam physics, where the concept of integration can be applied. This beam physics case study indicates that quantum integrations may arise, providing a stronger justification for exploring IIT through quantum means. Furthermore, if IIT can be understood through a quantum lens, this raises the possibility of using quantum resources to mitigate cognitive disorders and improve machine intelligence, with the potential for significant breakthroughs in these areas. Overall, this more refined notion of integration can bring us closer to understanding the intricate mechanisms behind human consciousness and perhaps even pave the way for significant advancements in cognitive computing. The tool is built upon the concept of a shallow embedding of C in ACL2, which allows for the translation of C code snippets by examining the local context in which they are used. The tool's functionality was demonstrated with a variety of examples including data structures such as linked lists and trees, as well as a simulation of a hard drive system capable of reading and writing binary values. Furthermore, this research paper outlines a methodology for creating the ACL2 representations of C code snippets that can be used with the tool to translate them into the target C code. The tool is available for public use at https://github.com/janjoost/shallow-c. The underlying ACL2 book can be accessed at https://github.com/janjoost/acl2-shdeep-subls. The source code for this content is included in the repository. The ACL2 parts in the tool outnumber the C code, allowing for the tool's functionality to be thoroughly verified and validated. The tool is designed to translate general and functional ACL2 code, whereas C code is translated only when accompanied by theorems to ensure correctness. The tool's verification is an integral part of its development process, which is why it uses a specific subset of ACL2 functions that is not exhaustive. As a result, this tool can be used to translate other programming languages within ACL2 by incorporating more functions, much like adding new features to a programming language. The tool's limitations are largely attributed to the absence of ACL2's set functions, which hampers its functionality in cases where lists are used as intended in programming. The use of functions ending in 'e' to iterate over lists is a workaround, but is often less efficient and more laborious than using regular set functions. As an example, the tool's simulation of a hard drive system is restricted from reading and writing lists of arbitrary length, which is why this example is more laborious and time-consuming than it could be if it utilized the full range of ACL2 functions. The use of set macros or a more comprehensive subset of ACL2 functions is necessary to translate generally structured programming ideas into executable C code. Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be categorized into 'enthusiasts' and 'casuals' based on their level of involvement with the platform. While both groups understand the purpose of a PIN, 'enthusiasts' made 2-3 times more, and 'casuals' had fewer than 2 additional attempts to access their account before giving up. A follow-up interview with 15 participants indicates that'enthusiasts' treat their PIN as a security feature but 'casuals' view it as a necessary annoyance. A key finding is that users might not utilize a strong PIN if they do not perceive it as a security measure, which highlights the importance of communicating a PIN's purpose effectively. Further research is needed to explore various factors that might influence 'casuals' behavior, such as the possible impact of users not utilizing a PIN as a security feature on relying on mass surveillance as a primary security measure, a particular concern in countries with restrictive online environments. A critical finding is that even though 'casuals' might understand the importance of security in general, they might not connect it to their use of communication platforms like Signal, which could be the case for a broader range of users as well. A possible research avenue is to investigate ways to effectively communicate a PIN's purpose to users, with a focus on users who understand security in abstract terms but struggle to connect it to their daily life, such as through the use of social norms framing in future work.

Numerous languages distinguish between forms of nouns based on gender. This characteristic poses a challenge to natural language models, compelling them to grasp the connections between words and their implied genders. We investigated how various models, including BERT and fastText, in a German context determine relationships between words, considering that agreements and discrepancies in gender affect these associations significantly. We discovered that the models tend to group words based on their agreements in gender, whereas those that utilize co-occurrence data, such as BERT and fastText, fail to accurately represent the implications of word relationships, falling back on statistical correlations instead. This means that the networks do not effectively capture subtle patterns in word relationships. We found the representations learned by BERT to be much closer to perfect than those of fastText, yet still imperfect, according to our criteria. This implies that the representations learned by BERT contain some form of implicit bias against female names. We discovered similar biases in the embeddings learned by fastFT, a representation technique employed by Agirrezabal-Oleta et al. (2018), which was designed to eliminate such biases. We found the embeddings developed from unsupervised methods to be free from these biases. We analyzed the local distributional properties of words, examining the contexts in which male and female names occur, to identify potential causes for these biases. We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their finite subgroups, properties of their center, and comparisons with related groups. Specifically, we show that if a finite subgroup of a group is highly repetitive, the group as a whole is also highly repetitive; further, we show that under particular conditions, the group's center will eventually become repetitive as time increases, and we resolve a longstanding issue regarding the repetition pattern in products of finite groups. Additionally, we apply our findings to characterize the attractiveness patterns in products of two finite groups, and extend these results to the context of measurable groups. Finally, we compare the attractiveness patterns in ourifiable groups and those that are not, and discuss some implications for the characteristics of their finite subgroups. All of these results are supported by various examples and counterexamples. Moreover, using our results about the attractiveness patterns in products of finite groups, we reproduce Furstenberg's original proof that certain sets are repetitive in nature. Lastly, to conclude our study, we compare the attractiveness patterns in certain groups with highly repetitive elements and those that are rigid in structure. Specifically, we show that under certain conditions, the group's rigidity and repetitiveness are not only compatible but also complement one another; further, we demonstrate a correlation between the attractiveness patterns in ourifiable groups and those that are stiff in nature. Ultimately, to further the knowledge in this area, we pose a series of questions that have the potential to advance the understanding of the characteristics of the group's repetition pattern. Estimating an object's pose is a crucial aspect of most visual pipelines in robots and 3D vision as a whole. This study tackles the challenge of accurately positioning new objects with no prior knowledge. This method builds on previous work by removing the necessity for object-pose-labelled data or category-specific 3D models during training. Additionally, we eliminate the requirement for 2D-3D projection during testing by utilizing self-supervised pose estimation skills. By employing a pose-encoding model that identifies an object's rotational orientation based on a pointcloud, we achieve this goal. This approach is successfully tested on the SUN3D dataset, yielding superior results compared to existing object-pose estimation methods. Furthermore, we also evaluated our method on the SUN3D split, demonstrating significant performance gains over other techniques. This work is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/UltimateV1nny/zero-shot-pose-estimation. Visual examples of our findings are presented in the accompanying video. Predicting short-term traffic is a widely researched area within intelligent transportation systems. However, existing forecasting systems face significant limitations due to their reliance on real-time data. The 2022 Traffic4cast challenge at NeurIPS addressed this issue by using publicly available sparse data. Our team submitted a solution to the expanded challenge of predicting estimated time of arrival. Our method involves extracting multiple feature sets - node flow characteristics, segment-based attributes, and similarity-based properties, which we used to train a model based on decision trees with gradient boosting. Our results demonstrate exceptional predictive capabilities across three cities - London, Madrid, and Melbourne - and even surpass some graph neural network-based approaches in estimating travel times. Our source code is available at https://github.com/c-lyu/Traffic4Cast2022-TSE.

VACA consists of two key components - a node representation sub-module and an edge representation sub-module, which collectively perform high-quality dimensionality reduction, according to our theoretical framework. Moreover, this framework derives an optimal-interventional VACA that effectively increases the causal query resolution rate. Our experimental findings demonstrate that VACA outperforms existing alternatives in counterfactual query resolution. Moreover, this work introduces novel metrics to assess the accuracy of dimensionality reduction, edge detection, and counterfactual query resolution within the context of graph structured data. State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) are now capable of producing massive data at speeds of hundreds of gigabits to terabits per second. This significant data rate complicates radio data analysis and necessitates costly computation. Although top-tier computing facilities are accessible for national and international institutions, local facilities operated by a single organization may not be equipped to handle these high demands. Given that the data rate of next-generation radio telescopes is anticipated to surpass current levels, local processing capabilities will grow increasingly crucial. We present REALTA, a computing system at the Irish LOFAR station (I-LOFAR) designed to record and process data in real-time and retrospectively. We also discuss several scientific projects hosted at I-LOFAR that utilize REALTA and highlight the benefits of in-house computing for local astrophysical research teams. Finally, we provide an overview of future plans to enhance REALTA to the LOFAR-CLASSIC scale.

Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to distinct radiation mechanisms. By analyzing the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray emissions from these blazars, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the complex astrophysical environment surrounding the blazar's core. This research employs a novel Monte-Carlo code called MAPPIES to simulate polarized patterns resulting from inverse Compton scattering of photons in a plasma cloud surrounded by a shock front. The code accounts for complex magnetic field configurations, photon and electron path alterations due to turbulence, as well as the effects of Faraday rotation and photoionization. In a previous study, researchers investigated shock wave properties and spectral energy distribution gaps, and now, using a comprehensive analytical framework, this study focuses on the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray frequencies in a scenario involving magnetic fields, plasma cloud thickness, and a gas region terminated by a shock wave. The predicted polarization patterns for various MAPPIES parameters were presented and compared to the observed polarization patterns of three blazars: 3C 279, NGC 1128, and PKS 1127-145. The application of this model to these systems reveals a compelling explanation for previously unaccounted polarization patterns in a particular magnetic field configuration and the spectral energy distribution characteristic of these blazars. Moreover, this study emphasizes that the polarization patterns resulting from external Compton scattering can provide substantial insight into the shock front's physical properties and the plasma cloud's dimensions, and these predictions are independent of the jet beam size and the accretion disk's position. Ultimately, the proposed model offers a unifying explanation for UV and X-ray spectral gaps and the predicted polarization patterns in a particular magnetic field configuration. Specifically, the proposed model is expected to yield considerable insight into shock front properties and the plasma cloud dimensions for a considerable range of its parameters and these predictions and the associated models can be extensively tested with high-resolution space and ground-based polarization observations of a considerable sample of blazars with UV and X-ray spectral gaps. A corresponding code for the strong Compton scattering in the hot accretion disk region is also being developed in a third paper. The systematic analysis and the systematic search for a considerable sample of blazars with UV and X-ray spectral gaps and the associated quasars may lead to a profound understanding of the complex astrophysical environment surrounding the blazar's core. This study aims to investigate how these waves could originate from early turbulence in the universe. It draws upon the connection between magnetic fields and the gravitational waves mentioned in a different scientific research, which states that the strength of magnetic fields shorter than the wavelength of 1 meter would produce parity-odd structures, which in turn would generate quadrupole fields that create gravitational waves. Calculations based on this model reveal that the intensity of magnetic fields at a particular scale would directly affect the frequency and amplitude of the generated gravitational waves, which explains why higher frequencies of magnetic fields would produce more gravitational waves within the Pulsar Timing Array frequency range. It has also been estimated that the magnetic fields responsible would possess energies equivalent to a small fraction of the energies produced by inflationary gravitational waves. This study further reveals that the magnetic fields at a particular scale would have reached their maximum energy density due to non-linear interactions roughly 1 second after the universe began to form, which is consistent with the possibility of detecting these gravitational waves using the Pulsar Timing Array method. It is also proposed that these gravitational waves could make up a significant part of the background noise observed within the Pulsar Timing Array frequency range if they originate from two different types of magnetic fluctuations, which have different scales, specifically the "magnetic relic" with 100--1,000 meters long strands, which has not fully decayed since the recombination period, and "magnetic fluctuations" with 1--102 meters long strands, which has a high re-cyclability rate. Light field technology is currently a focal point of interest for the digital entertainment and science communities due to its capabilities. Yet, the compilation and playback of high-quality light field images prove difficult due to their substantial data requirements. Recent studies on light field compression through estimation have shown promising outcomes, although they typically need substantial computing power or encoded data patterns during the compression process. Conversely, reversible compression techniques provide encoded patterns at an increased computational cost. This research develops a novel estimator-mapper scheme that enables the compression of light field images in a practical manner, regardless of the compression method utilized. It achieves this through a novel disparity-affecting model, enabling the coordination of 4D to 1D patterns more effectively and accurately. Furthermore, a practical lightweight approach to pattern-based reconstruction is proposed, allowing for the distribution of captured light field data into discrete encodable blocks using pattern encoding. These approaches combine to offer a realistic pathway to the compilation and playback of high-resolution 4D light field images on existing platforms. Experimental findings indicate that the proposed solutions enhance the efficiency of existing systems by a factor of 30 and offer performance comparable to the current top-rated systems under low-resolution conditions. It is noteworthy that our approach documents the first documented light field collection, the Yard collection, which amounts to 7 GB in full resolution. This research presents the first practical compilation and playback of LF images using a straightforward workflow, enabling the creation of high-resolution LF collections far surpassing current capabilities. It is available at a website, including videos and images. A related project involving the source code for the LF compression system is also available.

Most mainstream image compression methods, such as JPEG, are ineffective against the unique spatial-temporal properties of these image types. Conversely, the application of block-based predictive methods like JPEG-LS, and 4D-based approaches like BIP, have proven effective in compressing these image types. These image types are increasingly being compiled and played back on existing platforms due to recent advancements in light field camera technology and post-processing algorithms. However, the current pipeline of camera capture, compilation, and playback is often impractical on existing platforms due to their substantial data requirements.

The global health community relies on indirect estimates of health status and progress, which are frequently utilized at a small-area level. This study investigates the design and outcomes of three sequential estimates of infant mortality rates in Tanzania, beginning with the initial 2008 calculation by the National Bureau of Statistics and the World Health Organization. This work involves assessing the feasibility of conducting a survey to produce small-area estimates. The analysis compares and evaluates the estimates generated through a microsimulation model with those produced through conventional dissemination of larger-unit estimates to smaller areas. The findings suggest that model enhancements, specifically incorporating aggregation distributions and adjusting for estimation bias and inflation, yield more accurate results. Furthermore, incorporating geographically-based information in these models significantly enhances the accuracy of small-area estimates. This study indicates that applying these enhancements to standard two-stage estimates can result in improvements of up to 200%, and that conducting an additional survey to produce small-area data can result in further significant increases, up to 400%. These findings imply that the estimated 84,000 extra deaths reported in 2015 can be attributed to the lack of accurate small-area estimates. This study offers practical recommendations for improving the feasibility of small-area estimates in low and middle-income countries, which involve incorporating geographic information and enhancing the underlying data sources. These recommendations are expected to be particularly valuable in the context of global health initiatives. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a better position to inform the development of improved ADCs for the future, and advise against relying on the Zemax model, especially when blue spectrum accuracy is critical. We've also observed significant discrepancies between model predictions and our measurements, averaging 100 milliarcseconds, which highlights the need for on-site measurements to refine our understanding of atmospheric dispersion. This work has significant implications for telescopes and spectrographic instruments, and particularly those operating at the Extremely large Telescope due to its unique observing conditions. Future ADCs should consider incorporating accuracy measures for multiple models, allowing for the mitigation of atmospheric dispersion's effects on observational data. These results will inform the development of more precise ADCs, and we suggest adopting a new model which combines the predictions of several existing ones, or alternatively, creates a new empirical model based on our measurements that outperforms the current ones. Future work will focus on exploring the effect of atmospheric dispersion on spectrographic data, which could potentially provide additional information to supplement the existing models, leading to the development of more accurate ones in the future. Additionally, we'll carry out a detailed analysis of its impact on the accuracy of radial velocity curves, and we found that our measurements suggest that the Zemax model tends to slightly overestimate the atmospheric dispersion effect, which could lead to a 0.03 km/s discrepancy in radial velocity measurements. This paper employs a refined hierarchical latent variable model to capture patterns in multi-period time series data, which exhibit dynamics governed by various time-sensitive factors. Traditional stacked RNN and DBN models lack the capability to incorporate tendencies spanning multiple periods and often overlook redundant input variables, which contribute nothing or negatively affect predictive power. By integrating the hierarchical latent variable model with multiple transition periods and a Bayesian neural network equipped with Horseshoe priors as the input layer, our proposed method effectively filters out irrelevant variables, enabling enhanced dependency capture across varying temporal resolutions. Experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world data reveal a substantial improvement in modeling and prediction accuracy for multi-period time series data with our proposed method. Furthermore, our proposed model possesses a computationally efficient inference framework that accurately reflects the uncertainty in modeling estimates through posterior variance calculations. The model's efficiency in variable selection and robust performance on datasets with multiple periods of correlated input variables, as well as its capability to seamlessly integrate with a Bayesian neural network, make it a compelling option for time series forecasting tasks. The proposed method's code will be publicly available.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au and compared it to theoretical QRPA calculations employing the SLy4 Skyrme force. The measured strength distribution, alongside the nuclei's half-lives, is best explained by incorporating a combination of prolate and oblate configurations independently in the parent and daughter nuclei. Prolate components dominated both the parent and daughter nuclei, with the former exhibiting a more gradual and the latter a more abrupt strength decrease. A novel approach was also developed to analyze the direction of nuclear deformation during the decay process. It was found that the direction of deformation in $^{186}$Hg had an oblate shape, contrary to the normal expectation that this shape would persist in the daughter nucleus $^{186}$Au, with subsequent mixed calculations revealing a complex transition involving both prolate and oblate configurations in both nuclei. The interaction between these scalar fields influences both the dark matter relic density and the generation of baryon asymmetry through the right-handed neutrinos. We have developed a novel control method that learns complex systems quickly using extensive simulations, even with incomplete or imperfect data. This algorithm is designed to work with large datasets, user feedback, system models, and performance metrics to determine the best system design. To test its effectiveness, we applied this method to a series of complex control simulations. When given only one trial to learn to control a system, our algorithm successfully trained a human-like robot to perform challenging tasks such as reaching, swimming, walking, and flying. Moreover, our method can also optimize system design to meet specific requirements, as evidenced by our ability to customize a system's dynamics for additional purposes. This research highlights the potential of using advanced algorithms to design and control complex systems, and we believe that such approaches will play a crucial role in the design of future intelligent systems. The source code for this project has been made available on the Universal Learning repository. Additionally, we have performed an extensive set of experiments (55MB zip) and high-quality video trials (55MB zip), both of which demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. This research draws insights from the control of continuous-time systems, the theory of convex optimization, and the area of reinforcement learning with partial information. Specifically, we have improved the concept of policy optimization in reinforcement learning by addressing several limitations of previous frameworks, such as the need for user-provided reward functions or extensive simulation datasets. In addition, we have also leveraged ideas from data-driven control of continuous-time systems with partial information to accelerate the learning process in the absence of extensive data. This approach promotes the development of controllers that can operate with limited information, even when given only a few trials to learn to control a system. To test its effectiveness, we applied this method to a set of realistic control simulations. When given only a few trials to learn to control a system, our algorithm successfully trained a human-like robot to perform challenging tasks such as reaching, swimming, walking, and flying. Moreover, our method can also optimize system design to meet specific requirements, as evidenced by our ability to customize a system's dynamics for additional purposes. The results of this project have been recognized with a 2022 IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control Paper and the source code for this project has been made available on the Universal Learning repository. In addition, we have also tested and made available an extensive set of experiments and high-quality video trials. This research draws insights from previous work on data-driven control, partial information, reinforcement learning, control of continuous-time systems, and the area of policy optimization in reinforcement learning

In order to mitigate this problem, previous solutions employed practical approaches such as weight clipping and gradient penalty; however, these methods do not directly address the root cause of the problem. Recent research indicates that incorporating relational layers in the discriminator architecture can successfully alleviate the problem and enhance GAN training stability. In this work, we introduce a novel GAN architecture called relation GAN, which combines the effectiveness of relational layers and previous workaround techniques to provide a robust and stable training environment for GANs. Our architecture is an improved version of existing GANs, as it achieves superior performance on benchmark datasets such as CIFAR-10, CelebA, and LSUN, while requiring fewer epochs to converge compared to standard GANs. Notably, our architecture outperforms the current state-of-the-art GAN in terms of visual quality on the DTD dataset, which contains diverse and visually similar patterns. In order to facilitate replication of our experiments, we made our code and configuration available through a public repository. Our research suggests that relational GANs have great potential and can be extended to other layers, such as the generator, which could lead to new insights and a deeper understanding of the world. Consequently, using a combination of relational layers in both the discriminator and generator, along with a modified version of the standard adversarial loss function, allows the generator to produce photorealistic images. Consequently, it is essential to replace the standard loss function with a different loss function, which enables the generator to learn the real target distribution. Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework ignore the complexities of time. Factor loadings are treated as constants, unrelated to the conditions or events that shape an individual's life journey. This simplistic approach is hindered by the fact that factor loadings are affected by factors such as advancements in medical treatment and societal changes. We develop a non-classical factor model that accounts for the time-varying nature of factor loadings. Our approach is tested using data from four countries - Belgium, France, Germany, and Italy - where we build 20 separate models with variable factor loadings. Unlike traditional models, our method shows improved accuracy in forecasting mortality rates, particularly for the long-term. To facilitate widespread adoption, we create an open-source Mortality Forecasting Module with a user-friendly interface, integrating with the Shiny forecasting system. Our innovative model is applied in an interactive mortality forecasting environment where users can explore the impact of changing demographic structures, such as aging, on forecasting quality. Ultimately, our research illustrates the superiority of forecasting models with time-varying factor loadings over their static counterparts. Reducing the cost of neural architecture search (NAS) by sharing weights among different child models is a popular strategy. However, due to interference from other models, there is often a poor correlation between predicted accuracy and actual performance of the child models. This study investigates the cause of interference by comparing how similar the effects are when child models are trained with shared weights and reveals that the main factor determining the level of interference is the similarity in data distribution between the child models. Based on this insight, a new approach called "Symmetric Nas" is proposed to reduce the impact of interference. It involves creating pairs of models where the data distribution is similar, training them with a shared weight approach, and then combining them to generate higher quality architectures. Our experiments show that this method leads to a significant improvement in top-1 accuracy for both ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets. For instance, the top-1 accuracy on ImageNet is increased from 78.7 to 81.17. Our code can be found at the following repository: https://github.com/je-so-you-want-me-to-BLP/SNAS. Combining this with Leininger and Treibich's findings, we determine the boundary of a CAT(0) space: it must consist of a single point or be the union of a finite set of points and a tree's boundary. Furthermore, we present a new proof for a statement made by Leininger and Tishchev, stating that for a hyperbolic group $G$ acting on a CAT(0) space, the space's boundary corresponds to the set of $G$-stabilized vertices in its quotient graph. Additionally, we illustrate that the boundary being comprised solely of a tree's boundary points does not necessarily imply that the space is the covering action semigroup of a tree; this contrasts a result by the authors, established in a prior study. Lastly, we examine how our findings relate to the precision with which the boundary of a $V$-small length spectrum space can be defined. Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an extensively utilized method for evaluating the quality of machine translations by involving native speaker judges. Although prior studies investigate speakers' reliability in TQA, this study views judges as dependable translators rather than just evaluators. Consequently, it adapts an approach from psychology to evaluate the reliability of these judges. Initially, a standard translation model was developed using ratings from an established evaluation process, drawing on a large database containing translations and assessments from 30 judges. Subsequently, each judge's reliability coefficient was calculated based on this model, along with Bayesian measures of calibration and range. Lastly, we investigate how these measures correlate with various factors that impact a judge's reliability, such as their expertise, training history, and evaluation technique. It is discovered that certain factors have a significant impact on a judge's reliability, while others' effects are negligible. What is more, it is found that relying solely on calibration measures would cause one to overlook judges who possess high reliability despite their lack of high agreement ratings, and therefore, providing them with more consideration. Ultimately, we discuss the practical implications of these findings for the correction of machine translations. The study's code and data are available for public access on the GitHub repository.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types. We also explore relationships between intensity within bounded areas and wave frequency. Our work has been verified through numerical simulations in a diverse range of scattering configurations. In lotteries with exceptionally large jackpots, as seen in Mega Millions and Powerball,
increasing bettor participation actually works to reduce the return on investment for each ticket.
The reason for this is a higher likelihood of multiple people winning with the same ticket.
In an effort to boost the return on a lottery ticket, we suggest an alternative approach.
By dividing the possible winning combinations among different vendors and pairing them,
we minimize the chance of multiple people sharing the same winning ticket.
The results show that our strategy successfully raises the return on a lottery ticket
while also boosting sales, although it relies on the cooperation of all participants.
Furthermore, we've found the optimal time to launch this strategy, which is right before a
significant drop in the jackpot size, a common phenomenon in these types of lotteries.
Our research also reveals that pursuing the highest possible jackpot is a costly mistake.

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by the spherical nature of VMF distribution-based data, which cannot be properly represented by standard t-SNE. This limitation results in a range of inaccuracies, including a significant increase in spherical distribution approximation error and a substantial fraction of points exhibiting significant movement during embedding. This paper proposes a novel VMF distribution embedding (VMF-SNE) for spherical data for the first time. Developed on the back of the hierarchical Bayesian clustering approach, VMF-SNE can accurately capture the data's natural geometry. In comparison to other embedding techniques like K-SNE, VMF-SNE offers more efficient execution and more accurate representation of data characteristics. Its efficacy is validated through experiments on synthetic and real-world dataset examples, where it achieves a marked improvement in embedding accuracy and a minimal decrease in moving points when compared to its t-SNE counterpart. In addition, we provide a detailed explanation of how to configure the VMF-SNE model effectively. Finally, we discuss potential future research avenues for this model. Finally, we establish that the effectiveness of Scrum is influenced by both the benefits and drawbacks of working from home. Our findings offer valuable insights for practitioners and researchers that can contribute to future theoretical developments. Additionally, we address some limitations of this study and suggest potential avenues for replication. In pursuit of breakthroughs in the medical field, we analyze chromatic configurations in three-dimensional space, employing topological concepts. Leveraging techniques borrowed from image processing, we develop mathematically sound indicators to capture both fine-scale and broad-scale interplay among color categories. Our findings demonstrate that these new tools provide valuable insights into spatial relationships between different color groups within a photograph. Furthermore, we outline a potential application of these indicators to detect anomalies in medical imaging, specifically tumors in MRI scans. In addition, we show through numerical experiments that our method significantly reduces computation time in high-dimensional datasets, when compared to alternative methods. Specifically, alpha complexes and the simple persistent homology algorithm allow our method to analyze large datasets within a reasonable time frame. Lastly, we show both visually and numerically that our proposed indicators can detect a tumor in an MRI scan of the lungs. Our method succeeds in identifying the tumor where more traditional methods fail to provide meaningful results. Ultimately, the simple indicators yield the most impressive results among all our experiments. Lastly, we discuss how our research is closely linked to a promising area of study known as topological image physics. Certain types of images, such as those taken by satellites or cameras in space, benefit from our research. Additionally, we outline areas of future study including the detection of objects within datasets using a different indicator known as the beta cluster indicator, specific types of patterns known as rings and spirals, and a concept study on how to utilize the structure of color clusters to classify objects. This framework enables the creation of sets that aggregate more general categorization information, enabling a deeper examination of its capabilities in comparison to vector-space-based methods, which have previously been used for this purpose. Notably, the framework's feasibility and effectiveness are demonstrated using two case studies involving real-world audit datasets sourced from the Castleman and NYC audits. This framework offers several potential applications beyond auditing, including taxation, the classification of medical records, and the evaluation of program quality. This method could be particularly useful in situations where financial services and organizations are subject to tax inspections. Due to its versatility, this method could be applied to various sectors for the accurate placement of transactions within their respective categories. The framework's efficacy in this context is supported by empirical evidence, suggesting its potential to be a reliable solution for this specific problem. One significant advantage of this method is its ability to perform well even in environments where there's a significant amount of noise and limited resource availability. This makes it a promising candidate for a wide range of practical applications, particularly those involving the accurate placement of transactions within their respective categories. The results of this study highlight an alternative approach using conceptual knowledge for the placement of transactions within their respective categories. This method bears a resemblance to vector-based approaches in several key ways, yet offers a level of semantic meaning that's absent in these alternative methods. The use of complex information aggregation theories enables a more nuanced understanding of how general categorization information can be effectively aggregated. This study offers a valuable contribution to the field of text categorization through the application of this novel framework. In the context of string theory and quantum gravity, the Generalized Uncertainty Principle revealed the presence of an inherent minimum length, confirmed through the deformation of Heisenberg's algebra. Utilizing this concept, the transformations of Galilean and Lorentz Symmetries were investigated to determine the effects of the GUP on particle velocities. The research indicated that velocities near the speed of light in the galilean regime and the relativistic regime could be distinguished only when the characteristic length $\lambda_0$ exceeds the proton radius, and that the speed of light is a nonlinear function of $c$ in the Lorentz regime. Additionally, the GUP was shown to introduce an inherent distance of transcendence beyond which we cannot measure distance. A mathematical expression was developed for this transcendence distance in terms of the GUP parameter and $c$. Consequently, two more general transformations were proposed; the General Galilean Transformation and the General Lorentz Transformation, which subsumes both the Galilean and Lorentz transformations, and reduce to these latter when the GUP parameter is set to zero. Finally, using the General Lorentz Transformation, a expression for the GUP parameter was determined in terms of observable quantities, $m$,  $R$,  $\lambda_0$,  and  the velocity of the particle $v$. The findings reveal that measurements below a certain threshold, given by $\lambda_0$, are required to confirm the GUP, and that measurements above this threshold can confirm the GUP, and the results of such measurements can be predicted in advance. The research produces a fundamental understanding of the nature of space, time and matter at the quantum gravity scale. The research was carried out in the laboratory of Professor Basil G. Demianov. Building on Hall, Leung and Li's 2016 model for shared processing multitasking, this research extends the model to a more complex setting with parallel machines. Unlike the original model, where a set fraction of processing capacity is allocated to routine jobs, this extension allows for varying fractions of routine jobs' processing capacity to be assigned on each machine. The primary objectives remain the minimization of makespan and total completion time. Unfortunately, it's demonstrated that solving these problems optimally using polynomial time unless P=NP if machine ratios are fully adjustable. Conversely, it's possible to devise efficient solutions for machines with predetermined minimum processing allocations per machine when the machine number is constant. Further investigation is suggested into applying these results to various other job allocation problems. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions, a feedback control system was employed using feedback linearization. As a result, the robot successfully tracked the desired trajectory, reached the desired height in the simulation, and demonstrated the ability to extend its stride time. Even though the RFT model made assumptions about the robot's behavior, it yielded an acceptable level of accuracy when compared to the DEM simulation. Nevertheless, it was observed that the RFT model's predictions became increasingly inaccurate as the robot progressed through its hopping cycle. This study's findings have significant implications for the control of legged robots moving on deformable terrain. Future work will involve modifying the RFT model to improve its accuracy and applicability. In addition, a control system using model predictive control will be developed and tested to establish benchmarks for the limitations of feedback linearization. These achievements will pave the way for controlling robots using force and impedance feedback in various applications. Furthermore, this study will contribute to developing advanced models of deformable terrain that can be used in robotics and biomechanics. Such advancements are essential for the successful implementation of legged locomotion in diverse fields. In the rapidly evolving landscape of Internet of Things (IoT) networks, periodic firmware updates are vital for maintaining optimal security and reliability. Given the trend towards implementing security measures via code updates and the vulnerability of compromised devices to future attacks, investigating the outcome of such updates is crucial. Primarily, firmware upgrades are plagued by a success rate variable in wireless communities, a phenomenon known as "failures in the air." In this context, our research initiates a thorough exploration of the effect of such updates on large-scale IoT networks. To this end, our study employs realistic simulation environment, a shared mesh network architecture, and a moderate-scale IoT setting. Consequently, our analysis reveals that large-scale IoT networks undergoing periodic firmware updates are likely to experience outages and a decrease in performance. In response, our proposed resource allocation strategy is designed to mitigate such performance degradation and ensure seamless large-scale IoT networks. In particular, our approach is centered on adapting and leveraging successful packets from previous updates to improve the overall network in subsequent large-scale IoT firmware updates. By refining the choice of radio frequencies and transmission times, our method effectively enhances the large-scale IoT network's efficiency. In so doing, our study overhauls the large-scale IoT firmware updates and sets the stage for future work in this area. We employ a recursive Green function approach to obtain the Fock space propagator and associated self-energy for one-dimensional interacting fermions in a random potential. Our results show that the local self-energy's imaginary part, which governs the decay rate of initially localized states, can serve as a transition parameter to define the many-body localization phase transition with infinite precision. Additionally, the real and imaginary parts of the local self-energy display distinct, non-uniform scaling behaviors on either side of the transition, which is consistent with the concept of multifractality in the eigenstates. Conversely, the propagator's scaling behavior exhibits uniformity throughout the transition and is applicable throughout the applicable parameter range. Furthermore, the real and imaginary parts of the propagator's scaling exponent do not converge to their respective universal values until a significantly higher wavenumber than that of the self-energy. This suggests that the phase transition's characteristics are relatively stable over a broad wavenumber range that far exceeds the applicable Dyson method for this specific scenario. Lastly, a detailed analysis of the eigenstates' multifractal properties based on the $y$-expansion method once again confirms their consistency with the concept of multifractality throughout their entire property range. However, the eigenstates exhibit universality in their behavior only when the wavenumber reaches a relatively high enough range of approximately $1/k_{\frac{1}{2}}$. Consequently, the applicability of the entire Dyson method for the calculation of the many-body localization phase transition's characteristics is likely to be sufficiently sufficient. Nevertheless, the propagator's scaling approach does not require the use of the Dyson method and can be applied to other methods such as the variational Monte Carlo method for the calculation of the many-body localization phase transition's characteristics. Furthermore, the maximum possible precision in the calculation of the phase transition's characteristics as deduced from this propagator's scaling approach applies to all other types of the imaginary local self-energy, regardless of the method's type and type of potential. The propagator's scaling approach for the calculation of the many-body localization phase transition's characteristics as based on the local self-energy can be applied to higher dimensional systems and the implications of the concept of multifractality in the calculation of the phase transition's characteristics are discussed. To make the most out of human insight, interactive graph search groups specific labels in a structured framework that benefits image recognition, product organization, and database retrieval. However, current research mainly focuses on finding a single target within a graph and lacks a method for identifying multiple targets and their connections. This study introduces a novel technique for locating and differentiating multiple targets in a graph through a budget-friendly, interactive process. By employing a specialized data structure called a cover tree, the technique allows for efficiently selecting and narrowing down target options with the assistance of a human participant, and then leveraging label dependencies to determine the most likely target labels. The technique is validated through a series of human-in-the-loop multiple object search experiments. As a result, the technique successfully identifies 70% (or more) of all target nodes at a budget constraint of 20 minutes. Additionally, the technique is applied to a real-world dataset from the Stanford Online Organizer website, achieving an image classification accuracy of 64% by selecting only 10% of all image labels at a budget constraint of 10 minutes. By comparing the introduced technique with current end-to-end machine-based target localisation methods, the experimental results indicate a significant reduction in the time required to find targets by at least 93%. Consequently, the technique is suitable for areas where fast target localisation is crucial, and the use of a human participant is necessary to compensate for the limitations of machine-based algorithms. The exploration of quantum machine learning has demonstrated the potential for
groundbreaking insights in both areas of research. Experimental findings indicate
that quantum computers could significantly outperform traditional machines in
certain machine learning tasks, although they may also be resistant to some
adversarial attacks. However, there has been a gap in research on how these
vulnerable quantum models react to perturbations. Our study discovers
characteristics of quantum classification algorithms that make them particularly
susceptible to perturbations. We develop universal perturbations capable of being
applied to any quantum state, defeating a quantum classifier with a $99.79\%$
success rate. Moreover, we create adversarial examples for quantum classification
algorithms using a novel approach based on gradient-free optimization, resulting in
sample-wise perturbations that maximize the loss of the model. Our method
demonstrates that small perturbations can significantly impair the performance of
quantum classification algorithms. With the potential of quantum machines reaching
equal to or surpassing human-level performance, it is crucial to address this
vulnerability to ensure the reliability of these models when they are deployed.

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data. A proposed approach called frg can compare partial process runs by dividing them into start and post segments and comparing each segment against a reference model, using the results to compute a conformance measure. In experimental contexts, the technique was tested with real-world process data to examine its performance in assessing conformance and to investigate how the length of fragmented process runs affects the accuracy of alignments. A comparison of the technique with another method to assess conformance, called FPGA, showed that it generates a higher number of alignments with less computation time. Furthermore, the results suggest that the technique can effectively evaluate conformance with varied reference models, including those that partially or fully define process behavior. Overall, the research validates the technique as a reliable method to assess conformance with process executions and to analyze the technique's limitations with process runs that partially deviate from reference models. A discussion of the research and its limitations along with its potential to help analysts interpret and compare process executions is also included. A process guide to assess and evaluate the technique with process data is also created. A demonstration of the research is performed at the Conference for Advanced Research in Process Engineering in 2022. A complete implementation of the research is publicly available through Git at https://github.com/processanalyzer/conformance-assessment and can also be accessed through the developer portal of the researchers at https://processanalyzer.github.io/. Furthermore, the researchers created a simplified, interactive version of the research that can be accessed through the researchers' website at https://processanalyzer.github.io/frg-alignments/. Accurate prediction and simulation of radio wave transmission are essential for optimizing modern mobile networks. Existing propagation models are broadly classified into two types - empirical and deterministic models. Empirical models, although computationally simple, are often inaccurate due to oversimplifications in their statistical basis. In contrast, deterministic models, which use physics-based equations, provide superior predictions but require computationally intensive calculations. A new approach combining the strengths of both methods, referred to as Data-Driven Propagation Modeling, utilizes data on radio wave transmission collected from real-world environments and trains advanced machine learning algorithms to create precise propagation models. This novel approach is based on a unique two-step process, where a First Step Model estimates the signal strength in a coarse grid of locations, and a Refinement Imputation Procedure uses the results to improve predictions in finer grids. This article presents the first large-scale application of Data-Driven Propagation Modeling methods, where it combines a geomagnetic-based first model and a first-step model, along with a convolutional neural network-based refinement procedure, to create a highly accurate propagation model for 28 GHz. The resulting model has achieved remarkable accuracy, consistently estimating signal strengths within a 5 dB margin in 90% of nearly 500,000 Imputation Samples used in the training process. The model's effectiveness was evaluated based on a 28 GHz outdoor campaign in a downtown Manhattan location, providing results that compare positively when accounting for the coarse grid step size of approximately 5 meters. The same study also validates the robustness of the model against diverse typical outdoor scenarios, while demonstrating its capacity to easily adapt to different antenna types by adjusting a single parameter. In addition, the model's complexity, implemented using MATLAB code, is shown to be equivalent to that of only two conventional propagation models combined. Ultimately, the model's flexibility allows for easy adaptation to other frequencies through adjustment of a single broad-band parameter. The model's source code is available for free download on GitHub at https://github.com/antoniomulisch/28-GHz-Data-Driven-Propagation-Model. A precompiled Windows and MATLAB installer can be obtained from https://sites.google.com/apps.state.uus.edu/antoniomulisch/home. The model's website provides a web-based demo at https://antoniomulisch.github.io/28-GHz-Data-Driven-Propagation-Model. The site also hosts a comprehensive tutorial on Data-Driven Propagation Modeling and the related source code for the entire project at https://sites.google.com/apps.state.uus.edu

A straightforward semantics is proposed for temporal planning. High-level logic and decision procedures are utilized to determine the feasibility of achieving given goals within a specified time frame, and this capability is essentially an implementation of Brogaard's definition of time sensitivity. We have formally proven that our non-parametric time-invariant planning algorithm produces solutions that meet the proposed semantics, and that failure to find a solution under a specific search parameter indicates the goal is unattainable according to the semantics. Additionally, it is shown that our algorithm's behavior can be assessed through model checking, and an instance with a fixed world history can be created when the goal is unattainable. These findings are based on a comprehensive formalisation of the planning task, and our results are applicable whether the agent's actions affect time. We have validated the correctness of our development using the Coq proof assistant.  Our approach is unique as it is the first to provide a formally defined and formally validated planning framework grounded in intuitions from formal logic.  The framework is flexible since it covers a range of planning models, and it is scalable as it is based on widely-used decision procedures.  However, some of the previous results we discuss are potentially useful in areas outside of automated planning, such as cognitive modelling.  Furthermore, while the validation of our framework is currently restricted to a decision procedure that doesn't take time into account, future work could involve integrating time-aware decision procedures, and this could involve a more challenging verification process.  Eventually, once the integration is completed, we can confirm whether the decision tree-based approach to planning time has been formally validated.  This means not only will we get a theoretically-grounded understanding of the planning algorithm's semantics but also potentially, a way to improve its performance by reducing the size of the search space.  Ultimately, this means our framework could be useful for developing automated planning solvers that meet established semantics, and this could lead to applications in complex domains where understanding the meaning of the planning solution is crucial.  The primary limitation of our research is that it currently doesn't cover recursive time functions, and we suggest methods to overcome this challenge in future work.  Also, while the search-based verification approach provides a useful way to validate the planning semantics, we might be able to provide an even stronger verification guarantee, and this could lead to further improvements in performance by reducing the size of the search space. Power system expansion planning models, used to integrate renewable resources, rely on complex optimization problems involving various economic and technical factors. These factors carry significant uncertainties, yet their impact on model accuracy is poorly understood. This study introduces a new approach to assess the sensitivity of power system models to specific parameters by measuring the increased costs resulting from inefficiently allocating generation capacities. Through case studies involving capital costs, varied weather conditions, and differing spatial and temporal resolutions, we demonstrate the method's value and reveal that models are most susceptible to temporal resolution. Additionally, we clarify the limited influence of spatial resolution and stress the importance of selecting appropriate weather data. The development of this sensitivity analysis methodology enables planners to make more informed decisions when conducting economic dispatch and power system expansion planning, and more broadly serves as a general framework for assessing the impact of parameter uncertainties in optimization problems. The associated code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/MahdiMazraa/Sensitivity_analysis_for_power_system_models. The code can be replicated with the help of the OpenSource decomposition optimization solver, DOcplex (for complementary numerical results), and the high-performance solver, Bonmin (for optimal power flow calculations). Both of these essential tools form part of the larger COIN-OR-BCP suite, a widely-used, high-performance decision-making tool. For further validation, the decision-making tool, CPLEX, a leading commercial solver, was utilized. The associated registration information is available at https://coin-or.org/. This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov-Poisson and the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models within confined areas, under specified boundary conditions that include a particular reflection scenario for the Vlasov equation. We further prove a large family of moments' results, which enables the construction of solutions through the method of moments under certain initial conditions and moment constraints. We also show that this moment method can be applied to the Euler system to determine the limit of its scaled model's solutions. Furthermore, the Euler system is found to be convergent in a perturbative analysis of the ionic Vlasov-Poisson model under given small and regular initial conditions. Consequently, the study confirms the well-posedness of all three models within confined areas under presented initial and boundary conditions. Moreover, the study reveals that the charge conservation law governs the behavior of solutions in all three models. The study is performed with support from the ANR project "Modèles Mathématiques pour des Systèmes de Communication Robustes" of the French National Center for Scientific Research. A supplementary document of the study, focused on the regularity of planar domains' boundaries, is also available.

Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels, unique for their ability to be manipulated and modified dynamically through exposure to high-frequency sound waves. Studies involving colloidal gels revealed that by introducing these vibrations, several notable changes occur. Firstly, the rigidity of the gels significantly decreases. Additionally, the previously stationary phase boundary between solid and liquid states now responds and changes shape in response to the vibrations, while the molecular structure of the gel remains intact. Furthermore, simulations suggested that this phenomenon results from the disruption of the rigid three-dimensional network by resonating particles, causing a significant reduction in mechanical strength and ability to support weight. Interestingly, vibrations' effect on gel flow also exhibits an unusual pattern, in which the gel initially flows in a specific direction before eventually reaching a state of isotropic flow, during which the gel flows in multiple directions simultaneously and exhibits reversed flow properties, an effect attributed to the breaking and reforming of bonds within the gel structure, as particles collide and interact at microscopic levels. This unique behavior is explained by the introduction of "active forces" acting between particles, which significantly influence gel mechanics and dynamics. This study introduces a new class of materials with unique properties, reducing their yield stress by several orders of magnitude. This work facilitates ongoing research into the vibrations' effects on gel mechanics and dynamics, and raises exciting possibilities for dynamically modulating material properties in industrial and technological applications. Moreover, it sets the stage for further investigations on the long-term consequences of ultrasonic vibrations on gel flow and mechanics, as well as the potential to tailor material properties through vibration treatments. Ultimately, this can lead to a greater understanding of the complex relationships between network structure, flow mechanics, and dynamic properties. Furthermore, this work highlights the rapid advancements in materials engineering achieved through the synergy of theoretical and experimental frameworks. By combining advanced numerical simulations with cutting-edge acoustic rheometry, researchers can uncover hidden aspects of gel dynamics. This study proposes a new research direction: investigating the long-term effects of ultrasonic vibrations on gel flow and mechanics, which could lead to a broader class of materials with improved flow characteristics. Moreover, it highlights the significant potential of acoustic rheology as a powerful tool to uncover these dynamics. Future work can leverage this acoustic framework to develop smart materials with unique flow characteristics that can effectively adapt and change in response to various internal and external factors. This concept of material adaptation holds promising applications in multiple fields and can potentially lead to a transformative impact in materials science and engineering. Currently, classification primarily relies on human expertise, but semi-supervised Machine Learning algorithms can aid this process by utilizing labeled data to predict subject classes for previously uncategorized documents. Despite their assistance, these machine-driven classifications often lack clarity as to why they were made. Research into explainable AI aims to make Machine Learning more transparent by shedding light on the underlying decision-making processes. Building on the success of this technology with texts from fields like law and medicine, researchers are developing novel approaches for the classification of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) texts, which, due to their integration of both textual and mathematical content, pose an analytical challenge. In this study, initial efforts towards making STEM document classification more understandable are presented using state-of-the-art Mathematical Entity Linking techniques. Our findings illustrate the potential of these techniques to connect mathematical formulas within STEM texts to their respective knowledge graphs, thus offering a clear line of reasoning for classifications. Although the study's results are still in progress, we have achieved an understanding rate as high as 43% for a comprehensive set of STEM documents and 69% for scientific articles alone. With these outcomes serving as the foundation, we plan to further improve this technology and apply it to classify both digital and physical collections within the STEM field and its various sub-domains. Our long-term objective is to make this technology accessible to public search engines, enabling them to provide users with detailed descriptions of the mathematical content within uncategorized or off-topic documents. Ultimately, this move is key to advancing STEM openness and fostering open-access principles. For the time being, a live demonstration of our technology is available at https://math-ask.github.io.
