Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM. Furthermore, our findings reveal that this modification results in mass conservation to six orders of magnitude more stricter than the commonly employed Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy condition, while total energy is constrained to the same standard value. As an additional benefit, this modification also eliminates any torque resulting from unrealistically placed gravitational forces by maintaining compatibility with classical gravity for off-grid particles. Numerical studies have shown how the polarization of a proton is transferred in a specific collision event: $e + \vec {p} \to e + \vec {p}$. This investigation took into account the distortion of the proton's target, as well as the photon's interaction with the proton via the electromagnetic form factor. The results obtained revealed that the polarization of the proton is transferred in a certain probability, ranging between 7% and 35%, depending on the energy momentum $t$. This range of $t$ varies between $4 \times 10^{-3}$ GeV$^2$ and $16 \times 10^{-3}$ GeV$^2$. The probability found was notably higher when the electron's energy was increased, as long as $t$ was within the range of $10^{-3}$ to $16 \times 10^{-3}$ GeV$^2$. Furthermore, the polarization of the proton was shown to be more likely to occur when the squared $t$ momentum is less than $14 \times 10^{-3}$ GeV$^2$. This could be due to the electromagnetic form factor, which exhibits a dipolar structure that is related to the proton's spin transition from $uud$ to $suu$. The coefficient of this form factor is directly linked to the combination of isospin states, as $u^2-s^2$. This is significant because such a product yields a non-zero contribution to the polarization when the electron's energy is not at its minimum. This is where the polarization of the proton is transferred in a significant manner. On the other hand, the coefficient is zero at its most minimal value when the electron's energy is its lowest, resulting in zero polarization of the proton at that point. Additionally, the analysis showed that the distortion of the proton's target, as described by the $Y$ function, plays a crucial role in this phenomenon and reduces the probability of the polarization transfer compared to the scenario without target distortion. Specifically, the distortion results in a reduction of the probability ranging between its lowest and highest values, which are 0.07 and 0.35, respectively. Finally, the analysis considered the angle dependence of the polarization of the proton and the electron, as well as its dependence on the energy momentum $t$. This resulted in a notable dependence on the angle in the electron scattering plane, resulting in higher polarization at higher angles. Conversely, the polarization was shown to be minimal and independent of the angles in the perpendicular plane

We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning approach, a fundamental component of various learning techniques, is our focus, as it leverages the expertise of a guiding model to shape a student model's behavior. In order to accomplish this, we implement our proposed method, augmented policy cloning, which introduces artificially generated states to a training environment, making the system sensitive to its surroundings, thus greatly reducing the need for direct interaction with the environment for the learning model to perfectly replicate its mentor's actions. We achieve highly efficient behavior transfer from experienced to novice models utilizing this method. We evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed technique in transforming a models' behavior even in scenarios where the models have highly defined and restricted behavior and also when the models the models are trying to mimic have highly defined and restricted behavior and observe compelling results in both cases. Moreover, we validate the underlying reasoning behind our approach by deriving the conditions under which our method is most effective in producing useful data for the learning model to perfectly emulate its mentor's actions. We demonstrate that our method in its current form has its drawbacks and limitations and that exploring alternative data augmentation techniques could yield even better outcomes in certain cases. In particular, the method in its current form is not suitable for and shows poor performance in scenarios where the models have highly defined and restricted behavior and this could be resolved by implementing a different data augmentation technique that yields better results in these cases. Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities.
This technology, in conjunction with phase-coherent feedback from detected signals to modulation, enables the creation of a resonant spin maser system highly sensitive to changes in background magnetic fields.
Our system incorporates digital signal processing integrated into the maser feedback loop, thereby meeting the necessary phase condition for resonant precession.
Using a compact laser and mass-produced caesium vapour cell, it functions effectively in a 50 microtesla field and has the potential to be applied in portable geophysical magnetic field measurements.
Our results show a Cramer-Rao limited resolution of 50 fT at 1 second sampling rate and a 10 kHz bandwidth, indicating a suitable resolution for precise measurements.

Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms lacking a Siegel disk can be constructed to have a Picard number of 2, thereby confirming a long-standing conjecture of Bogomolov. Additionally, the technique of hypergeometric groups is used to construct a family of K3 surfaces, where each member's automorphism possesses a Siegel disk and the associated Picard number is 2. This family's characteristics include an automorphism of intergral type with a large translation determinant and a non-identical fiber in one of its 22 possible systems, where each system corresponds to a different eigenspace under the automorphism's action. Furthermore, for any given value greater than 23, we can construct a K3 surface whose automorphism possesses a Siegel disk, the Picard number is 2, and the determinant of the matrix representing its action on a basis is that given value. However, for any given value less than or equal to 22, we can construct a K3 surface whose automorphism possesses a Siegel disk, the determinant of the matrix representing its action on a basis is less than or equal to 22, and the Picard number is 2. A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results. A parallel implementation using the $\mathtt{B Bellhop}$ library on $\mathtt{40}$ NVIDIA V100 GPUs shows the algorithm outperforms $\mathtt{B Bellhop}$'s SGD and SDAG implementations, and matches or surpasses solving $\mathtt{20}$-dimensional Newton steps on a single GPU with CUDA. Furthermore, the algorithm's effectiveness is shown in comparing against $\mathtt{B Bellhop}$'s SGD implementation on a $\mathtt{2021}$ MacBook Air with CPU solving $\mathtt{40}$-dimensional logistic regression. 

Key Words: distributed machine learning, stochastic Newton algorithm, logistic regression, convergence analysis, parallel computing, GPU optimization, MATLAB and C utilities.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino floor, or distinguish between various neutrino sources. With sufficient readout detail, such as when employing micro-pattern gaseous detectors, Time Projection Chambers can allow directional recoil detection. The main issue with these detectors is identifying and eliminating backgrounds caused by non-recoil charged particles. We propose introducing specific physical quantities that focus on local spatial and temporal relationships between charges, greatly increasing the ability to distinguish recoil directions while minimizing influence from non-recoil backgrounds. Our proposed method was tested using simulated data from detectors detecting both dark matter and background particles in a in-depth simulation. The simulation showed that these new physical quantities lead to a high success rate of directing recoil tracks, with more than 90% remaining directionable after background interference, while also reducing background influence to less than 10%. Ultimately, this approach could serve as a basis for our upcoming TESLA3 Test Stand's research protocol. The primary goal of this research is the direct detection of dark matter, with particular focus on detecting directions. The simulated analysis is of a 300 kg drift chamber with a 2 mm spatial resolution over a two-year run period. The results of this simulation show that using these new physical quantities results in a 20% improvement in ability to distinguish recoil directions while also increasing sensitivity to dark matter, specifically by a factor of five. The concept of integrating charge focus and concentration into the analysis has also been explored, resulting in a 30% or greater boost in ability to distinguish recoil directions. The concept of re-projecting simulated analysis results could potentially provide an additional 10% or greater boost. The results of this research were presented at JPGC2021. The related code for this research can be found at https://github.com/appliednumerical/recoilID. An updated version of this code, allowing for integration with the jeta2tpg framework, can be found at https://github.com/appliednumerical/recoilID/tree/reorient. The results of this research were presented at the 2022 Winter Meeting of the APS-DFG. A related talk was given at the 2022 Winter Meeting of the APS-DFG. The physical quantities proposed in this research were showcased in a visual context at the 2022 TPCvIII conference. The proposed research was presented at the 2022 Science Days event.

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior involves evaluating various personal characteristics and environmental influences. Current approaches to driver evaluation largely depend on subjective observations, which are prone to bias and may not accurately consider the situation at hand. In contrast, a more recent approach utilizes both subjective and objective information to create a more comprehensive understanding of driving behavior. However, some drivers' concerns about being unfairly evaluated due to personal circumstances still need to be addressed. In order to ensure fairness and accuracy in driver assessment, expert review should be implemented as a crucial part of the evaluation process. By involving experts, both the fairness concern and the uncertainty associated with the original assessment can be quantified, which in turn provides a more reliable and fair assessment that also considers the situation at hand. In this paper, we propose a novel method of outcome explanation and post-hoc justification for assessements that involves combining the expertise of multiple specialists. Our approach, which proposes multiple evaluation outcomes based on expert input, is evaluated using real-world driver assessment data, which shows that involving experts significantly improves the accuracy and fairness of the assessment. In addition, an analysis of the costs and benefits of implementing expert review reveals that it provides the best trade-off between fairness and precision. Ultimately, the proposed method could significantly impact a variety of fields that rely on evaluation as a crucial component, such as resource allocation, selection and promotion, and monitoring for biased behavior. In a broader context, our findings demonstrate the practical value of modern NLP techniques in real-world settings where accuracy and fairness matter. Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables move throughout a defined space. Determining shortest paths between points involves looking at various types of paths, including straight lines and curved lines. While straight lines are straightforward to analyze, the case for curved lines presents unique challenges due to its non-linearity. Notably, investigating the expectation of path costs in the curved case is particularly hard. Focusing on Gaussian models, we develop an initial resolution for this problem, revealing an unexpected connection to the properties of the underlying space. Additionally, we refine our solution by limiting our path structure, specifically when there are three or more points, to the simple geodesic line. Our analysis is further reinforced by a simulation that demonstrates how these results accumulate as the size of the data grows. Lastly, we expand upon this work by considering how to evaluate the accuracy of these results statistically. Specifically, we emit a call for further investigation into the (exponentially) increasing discrepancy between the analyzed case and the original, partially line and partially plane case. A complementary technical document has been made available.

In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.  A thin membrane separated two fluids with significantly different densities, situated above a curved upper surface. When triggered, the membrane drops and we track the resulting interfacial dynamics until turbulence develops.  Our focus lies on how the curvature affects linear instability and the transition to turbulence through the modulation of eigenmode growth due to periodic curvature influences.  If the curvature increases in one direction, it decreases in the opposite direction.  This work reveals how periodic external forces can accelerate the transition to turbulence over natural instability.  Periodic external pressures also bring on an earlier transition to turbulence.  This is an innovative method that offers a new approach in manipulating turbulence patterns through curvature manipulation.  This work fundamentally enhances our understanding of how external forces can affect instability in fluids and promotes a deeper comprehension of turbulence phenomena.  Moreover, this technology has vast applications and can be adapted in various areas such as drug delivery, material science, biology, and more.  Following this introduction, a more in-depth explanation of our experiments and theories will be provided.  In particular, we will show that periodic forces can also bring about unique spatio-temporal turbulence patterns that are characterized by specific wavenumbers, including 1/3.  These patterns originate from an interaction between the Curle-Housten effects and membrane stiffness.  If the curvature increases in one direction, it reduces in the opposite direction, causing an uneven stretching and thinning of the fluid film.  This leads to an increased adhesion energy that causes turbulence patterns with specific features.  In contrast, turbulence patterns caused by periodic forces in a controlled environment exhibit a broader spectrum of frequencies.  As a result, the characteristics of the turbulence patterns depend on the state of the environment but not the curvature.  In a controlled atmosphere, the curvature does not affect the frequency of the turbulence patterns.  This work brings together theories related to periodic forces, the properties of liquid films, and the effects of external forces, offering a more holistic understanding of turbulence phenomena.  In particular, the experiments reveal that a natural explanation for turbulence patterns observed in the laboratory and the causes of their diversity can be found.  In addition to experimental data, the work describes how the thickness of the fluid also plays a crucial role in the transition to turbulence.  This is an area of research that has not been well studied and the methods used in our experiments and simulations are an innovative approach to understanding this phenomenon

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(Z)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, we examine the standard twisted L-function, $L(s,F,\chi,St)$, and show that its algebraic component at critical point $m$ has bounded denominators as $\chi$ changes. This work refines a previous finding of Boecherer. A similar result also holds for the product of Hecke L-functions of primitive forms from the special linear group $SL_2(Z)$. This was done by combining elements with Jeandel's boundary estimate with recent developments from Wang's work on the invariance of Siegel modular forms under the symplectic group. The transport properties of spin-dependent systems are crucial in spintronics, quantum computing, and magnetic devices, and are typically influenced by the structure and magnetic properties of the system. We have theoretically investigated transport through non-cirulated graphene nanoribbons with ferromagnetic gates, showing that the spin-dependent current is highly sensitive to the nanoribbon's geometry, magnetic configuration, and electron energy. A notable feature is the appearance of spin polarized resonances that can be controlled using the Ferromagnetic Gate (FG) by adjusting its position relative to the nanoribbon. Utilizing the Non Equilibrium Green's function method, we evaluated the spin-dependent conductance of these graphene nanoribbons under bias and in the presence of FG gating effects. Our results indicate that the spin-dependent conductance exhibits a complex relationship with the FG's position, revealing three distinct behaviors: (i) a lack of conductance when the FG does not overlap with the nanoribbon, (ii) a dip in conductance when it overlaps, and (iii) a resonantly conducted spin-polarized charge, which can be adjusted by the FG. A prominent characteristic is that a considerable amount of conductance is maintained even in the presence of FG gating, and is accompanied by a variable degree of spin polarization that can be adjusted by the FG's position. Furthermore, the spin-dependent conductance exhibits a resonant behavior, and its polarization can be adjusted by the FG's position, and its resonance characteristics may hinder the achievement of ideal spin polarized conductance. Our study of the behavior of spin-dependent conductance in these graphene nanoribbons suggests that they could be used to develop sophisticated spintronic devices with adjustable properties. A notable aspect of these systems is their sensitivity to geometry, magnetism, and electron energy, and a crucial characteristic is that a considerable amount of conductance is maintained even in the presence of ferromagnetic gating. A potentially exploitable feature of these systems could be the achievement of ideal spin polarized conductance through the adjustment of ferromagnetic gating. A considerable amount of research has focused on transport properties of spin-dependent systems, and a major challenge is achieving ideal spin polarized conductance in the absence of ferromagnetic gating. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social attributes. However, a recent study that analyzed a large dataset of Chicago's taxicab trips discovered that changes in human behavior brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic decreased the diversity of urban encounters. Data from GPS-based trip records showed lower trip frequencies in areas with higher infection rates, particularly a $13\%$ decrease in areas facing severe outbreaks and a $26\%$ decrease in areas hit hard by the virus. Additionally, residents in infected areas reduced their exploration of other neighborhoods by $29-41\%$, which led to a significant decrease in the diversity of urban encounters. It was found that the diversity index, which measures a city's overall diversity by calculating the number of different areas a single individual visits, experienced an average decrease of $7\%$ after a month of reduced movement and further declined by $9\%$ after two months. Finally, analysis of the diversity of urban encounters indicated a strong, positive relationship between pre-pandemic diversity in a given area and the degree of decreased movement, which signified $25\%$ higher two-month diversity levels. Therefore, areas that were more diverse prior to the pandemic saw lesser drops in diversity during the pandemic period. A sensitivity analysis revealed a range of potential factors that might underlie the decreased diversity in urban encounters during the pandemic. It was concluded that additional public health measures are needed to mitigate increased health disparities brought on by the pandemic. Moreover, the fact that areas with higher diversity experienced less decreased movement indicated that diversity-enhancing urban planning policies might also play a crucial role in addressing health disparities. A deeper understanding of how diversity affects public health is also crucial for making more informed policy decisions. It's also revealedtravel patterns are influenced by various factors including age, which resulted in younger and older individuals exhibiting unique movement patterns during the pandemic. Consequently, a more equitable pandemic response could be achieved through age-targeted initiatives. Furthermore, the fact that work-related trips were heavily impacted by the pandemic highlights the significance of maintaining urban economic centers as hubs for post-pandemic recovery efforts. Ultimately, a more equitable recovery could be fostered by prioritizing under-resourced neighborhoods and ensuring the quick revival of urban economic areas. 

The research findings suggest policymakers should prioritize two key post-pandemic goals: maintaining diversity-enhancing urban features like public transportation systems, and fostering economic activity in central areas that were heavily impacted during the pandemic. fluid dynamics and transport within diverse porous media. A proposed algorithm,

initially, an approximate update of pressure and saturation is achieved through
a preconditioning step by resolving sub-problems in succession; secondly, a
global Newton update is applied at the preconditioned state via system linearization.

methods including MSPIN and conventional strategies like Sequential Fully Implicit

two times relative to SFI. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the preconditioner is

interfacial collapse, and flow into tightly grouped wells. A notable advantage of the
FSMSN method lies in its capacity to maintain stability even in problematic well-to-well
connections, which traditionally results in instability for SFI. Although performance
slightly surpasses existing methods like PNNLS-SFN, despite demonstrated robustness,
the FSMSN method does come with an additional computational cost compared to SFI.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). These techniques, such as primary axis transformation (PAT), rely on iterative training to improve prediction accuracy. However, they have significant drawbacks, including a high computational burden and the risk of overfitting, which becomes particularly problematic for larger quantum systems. To address these limitations, we propose a new MEM approach based on the unfolding technique commonly used in spectrometry. In contrast to PAT, our method benefits from a lower computational cost per iteration and is more resilient to overfitting. Additionally, it can handle more circuit-based regression problems more effectively. We demonstrate our approach's state-of-the-art performance by achieving 35% higher average fidelity and 10% higher average probability of a single qubit being correct, respectively, when applied to real quantum hardware. This method allows us to perform noise-reduced simulations of a 27-qubit quantum teleportation routine within 10 minutes. Furthermore, our approach's processing time is substantially less than 1 minute, which is fast enough to support noise-reduced simulations for most circuits on current 7-qubit quantum hardware. Overall, our approach makes it possible to perform reliable quantum experiments on current noisy quantum devices. When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to carry out. Current research on assistive control methods that enable robots to recognize human objectives focuses primarily on visual elements such as grasp position and orientation. However, studies have shown that humans primarily use arm movements to determine tasks, and not grasp-specific visual data. We conducted a study to explore how the structure of arm movements is utilized to infer tasks in situations of shared autonomy. We discovered that when humans control a robot arm, their goal becomes apparent from the integrated movements of all joint values, rather than solely grip positions or orientations. Our research presents the first method that can determine tasks by analyzing overall movement patterns, making no assumptions about the specific grasp or manipulation model. We assessed our approach on a dataset comprising four categories of tasks performed by casual operators, and found that it successfully identified the classes correctly 87% of the time. Additionally, we found that incorporating information on robot movement could enhance task classification by 10%. Our research suggests that effective communication of robot conventions through shared autonomy involves both clear human instruction and subtle cues provided by the robot. These shared perspectives on arm movements can lead to an understanding of task goals that is more accurate and reliable. We are releasing our code and dataset to support further advancements in this area. Such advancements could lead to the development of more conventional and consistent interactions between humans and robots, including the capacity to learn from new users without the need for extensive training. Ultimately, our research has the potential to contribute to the creation of a common linguistic and behavioral framework for human-robot collaboration. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and provide a complete environmental representation. A novel solution to address this challenge is the proposed Hierarchical Topological Map Representation (HiTMap), which focuses on large-scale mapping and graph structure to achieve this goal. By incorporating two levels of processing - one focusing on localization and the other on environmental feature extraction, HiTMap enables simultaneous map construction and navigation. Furthermore, the system leverages a dedicated node for state estimation and environmental feature detection, allowing it to navigate using a logical graph of landmarks and topological features. Evaluation of HiTMap was carried out using real-world data from a robot equipped with a head-mounted camera, comparing its performance with existing state-of-the-art systems. Results indicate that HiTMap achieves comparable navigation accuracy with state-of-the-art systems but significantly reduces computational load by 53.76%. Additionally, the findings show that HiTMap is more robust to changes in illumination conditions than the state-of-the-art systems. A notable advantage of HiTMap is its ability to navigate and reconstruct the environment's layout simultaneously. From a free energy model, we calculate the electrostatic potential and number of water and ions within the boundary using coupled differential equations, including the Poisson equation and a variable density equation for water and ions. We discover that solvent effects profoundly impact the electrostatic potential, ion distribution, and water content across the boundary, especially at low electrolyte concentrations. Furthermore, we investigate how surface charge density impacts the electrostatic potential, ion distribution, and water content across the boundary under different electrolyte concentrations. Additionally, we re-examine the free energy model and determine the free energy of the system in equilibrium on both the microscopic and macroscopic levels, resulting in a free energy that depends solely on the electrolyte concentration and surface charge density, thus corroborating the scaling free model. Lastly, we establish a relationship between the apparent capacitance of the boundary and the electrolyte concentration, effectively generalizing the diffusion capacitance model. We also suggest several possible experimental methods to verify our theoretical predictions from a capacitance-based perspective, inspired by recent research in graphene-water-electronite interactions. Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for researchers. To this end, we annotated a dataset based on a real-world use case from a company, and then trained a BERT model on a dataset comprising sentences annotated as requirements and non-requirements. After evaluating our model's efficacy, we discovered it performed slightly better when identifying true requirements among non-relevant sentences than when distinguishing requirements from one another. Notably, our results suggest transferring knowledge from one domain to another is more crucial than increasing training dataset size. To facilitate replication and advancement, we provide access to our code and dataset. Furthermore, we aim to make our solution commercially available as a cloud service. Using our solution, we were able to accurately extract a substantial number (414) of requirements from a 215 page long business requirement document, which significantly surpasses the count that could be achieved through manual extraction (122). By comparing our approach's extraction efficiency and accuracy to those of existing natural language processing and machine learning based methods, we demonstrated their respective abilities to extract requirements ranged from 1 to 20 per hour. Ultimately, we worked with the company to tailor our solution to meet their specific requirements, and then successfully validated it in a live setting. In particular, we leveraged our model to facilitate a substantial (7488) sentence reduction in a large project's requirement narrative, and then demonstrated its superiority over our initial model's performance on a broader dataset comprising 5212 additional sentences. To ensure the high quality of our extraction outcome, we maintained a consistent approach of providing the model with input and output annotations. Consequently, we discovered the model's predictions exhibited temporal and spatial coherence, and we attributed this phenomenon to the incorporation of contextual attributes. By designing various evaluation metrics to assess the outcome of our extraction approach for a 530 hour project, we were able to establish a positive correlation between its results and project quality, and thus verify the accomplishment of our solution. In contrast to our initial model's performance on a broader dataset comprising 5212 additional sentences, we noticed some outcomes with lower scores. To overcome these limitations, we took two key steps - adjusting the model's initial training to rectify these errors, and incorporating additional attributes to enhance the precision of our extraction. Specifically, we found that relying solely on the text is not sufficient for extracting requirement information effectively. To circumvent these challenges, we considered the feasibility of different auxiliary inputs, ultimately selecting a collaborative approach due to its high level of temporal and spatial coherence.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. A direct link between outage probability, energy consumption, and energy efficiency is established, followed by a formulation of the optimization problem to maximize energy efficiency under the constraint of maintaining a target outage probability. A practical scheduling and power allocation strategy is implemented to minimize power usage. Since the optimization problem is complex and difficult to solve, a tight approximation is first used to simplify the outage probability, then energy efficiency is re-expressed in a different form and the optimization problem is re-cast into a solvable form as a mixed-integer non-linear problem. A generalized outer approximation algorithm is then employed to find a solution to the optimization problem. When comparing the non-outage and outage-based energy efficiency, it is found that non-outage energy efficiency offers greater optimization possibilities. Furthermore, the best way to achieve energy efficiency is through a full deployment of cooperative diversity, which is accomplished by scheduling and power allocation optimization, specifically by allocating power to relays rather than the source. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme. Furthermore, it is observed that a moderate number of weakly effective relays is more beneficial than a few highly effective ones. Moreover, it is observed that the benefit of network coding in terms of energy savings is noticeable only at relatively high signal-to-noise ratios. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with.
Recent studies propose using Artificial Intelligence-based techniques but most
methods are one-dimensional as they rely on a single, large dataset, which is
not adaptable. A long-time goal in Machine Learning is to achieve Continuous
Learning - to become better without a complete reset. Our study showcases the
first instance of using Continuous Learning in Multiple Sclerosis lesion
segmentation, and we compare its effectiveness to training on scratch and using
a pre-trained model. Our findings indicate that Continuous Learning is better
than training from scratch, and equally or better than using a pre-trained
model, underscoring its value in models designed to analyze radiological images
of MS lesions. Moreover, we show that using Contrastive Learning enhances the
model's resistance to variations in datasets, protecting its performance even
when transferred to a new hospital's radiological images, where it encounters
lesions that were not present in its initial training dataset. Our study's code
will be accessible at: https://github.com/krizhanovski/continual-msseg. A demo
is hosted at: https. msseg-demo demos.ksu.edu. Our ongoing work can be viewed at
https. msseg-demo demos.ksu.edu/continual. Figures/tables are located at the
end of this file. Keywords: Continual Learning, Multiple Sclerosis segmentation,
Large-scale Self-Supervised Pre-Training, Medical Image Analysis, Artificial
Intelligence.

In the majority of machine learning applications involving physics-based data, the underlying models are assumed to perfectly represent their corresponding physical systems. However, in cases where models significantly diverge from reality, the learned connections can be overly optimistic and unreliable. Despite receiving considerable attention in recent years, the issue of learning from imperfect models remains relatively underexplored. This research develops a new framework for identifying and characterizing model errors in fluid dynamics. To achieve this, a deep learning approach is used to analyze input-output relationships in physical systems via various fluid dynamics simulations. One of the main challenges in identifying model errors is determining corresponding quantities in different fluid dynamics models, as the relative size of variables can make it difficult to establish equivalences. This issue is addressed by applying a novel input transformation that ensures feature mappings are within a unit circle with a well-defined geometry. Following the successful identification of model errors, the proposed framework allows for the adaptation of learned representations to accommodate multiple models, thereby facilitating tasks such as physics-based reinforcement learning and reducing the need for extensive online exploration. To demonstrate the efficacy of this framework, a basic example involving model error in laminar flow is first introduced, followed by a more complex case studying model error in the performance of continuous control tasks. These experiments include modeling the dynamics of a cart-pole system both with and without friction, resulting in significant improvements in sample efficiency for the no-friction case when using the proposed framework. Model error was also investigated in the adversarial environment of car-racing tasks, where the goal of the policy is to survive rather than achieve optimal performance. This investigation into model error in this case highlights the need for adversarial robustness optimization, as the presence of model error can lead to policies that are resistant to a antagonist's actions. Ultimately, the proposed framework provides a method for estimating model error and re-designing input features to minimize its influence. Experimental results indicate that this approach significantly improves the resilience of continuous control tasks to model error, and that the proposed input transformation has a range of applications in physics-based reinforcement learning. This research serves as a foundation for investigating machine learning in cases where models significantly diverge from their corresponding physical systems, and it is expected to have a significant impact on a variety of applications involving physics-based data. It is also expected to be a useful resource for researchers working to understand the relationship between physical models and their corresponding learning algorithms. Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, PASTA can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for natural language understanding tasks such as text categorization and named entity recognition while updating a mere 0.029% of all parameters.
Our contribution offers a straightforward yet efficient way to fine-tune models, with applications across various deployment scenarios for handling multiple tasks, and underlines the crucial importance of special tokens in pre-trained language models. Moreover, our approach makes it possible to handle tasks with numerous categories without any additional adjustments to the special token embeddings.
Lastly, PASTA's success highlights the potential for handling subtasks like named entity recognition using special token adaptation alone. To facilitate future research, we release our code at https://github.com/allenai/pasta. The code for fine-tuning with pre-trained models appears at https://github.com/allenai/fine-tune-language-models. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, which prompts the use of context-dependent preference modeling. To tackle this issue, we examine two distinct Siamese network designs, contrasting one that compares the resultant collections after an addition with another that considers each item's individual contribution to the existing collection. Moreover, when we analyzed the results of the user study, we noticed a considerable parity between the models in terms of preference rankings for specific instances, which highlights their potential for collaborative use to aid preference elicitation or serve as a companion in decision-making processes. Finally, combining the insights from the user study and various metric assessment methods with a thorough ablation study enabled us to offer some suggestions for further improving the future development of set-addition preference modeling. Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We examine this knowledge gap through a natural language inference task by creating a set of specialized questions from existing NLI datasets, which helps us assess a range of models' ability to understand these negation types. Our analysis indicates models perform notably well on some negation categories, revealing a significant distinction in their processing abilities. Furthermore, our findings highlight the potential for these models to leverage the increasing amount of online data to better understand various negation types, despite the models' limited performance compared to human experts. We make our dataset and code available for other researchers to build upon. Our models' performance can also serve as a useful benchmark for future research. We discuss implications of our results, suggesting integration of more negation types from developmental psychology into the current models' training. We aim to bridge the understanding gap between the developmental and AI communities, contributing to the former's theories and the latter's ability to develop more effective AI systems in the future. We explore these contributions as part of the GEODE Research Action at the Alliance of Science for the Future. We provide the following resources online: \begin{itemize} \item Developmental Negation Processing Transformer Code - This code demonstrates how to employ a transformer model for the task and successfully replicates our experiment using the full dataset. We establish a consistent training, testing, and hyperparameter setup for future researchers to build upon. \item Developmental Negation Processing Transformer Data - This includes our fully automated dataset creation process using existing NLI datasets. We generate and report results for over 30 different types of developmental negations. We measure models' performance across different training corpus sizes and learnability. We analyze these factors through both human and machine processing. \item Developmental Negation Processing Transformer Results - We provide and analyze the results for various transformer models, including the highly influential ones from the SuperGLUE benchmark. We also provide the results for non-Transformer baselines, comparing their performance alongside. \end{itemize} We discuss these findings and identify the next steps for integration. Finally, we bring together the theories from developmental psychology and the research on AI systems, establishing a more comprehensive understanding of both fields. As part of the GEODE Research Action, we aim to develop more effective AI systems and contribute to the understanding and implementation of AI as 'cognitive-welfare system'.

To address this, we propose a novel look-ahead attention framework that aims at mimicking how humans translate by looking ahead to the complete translation and then iteratively refine it. Our method utilizes an innovative structure, incorporating a novel look-ahead mechanism and a novel loop structure, to refine translations. Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies the CTMC framework, calculating the inverse Z-transform and inverse Laplace transform separately for discretely and continuously monitored options. As a result, we achieve improved explicit Laplace transforms, surpassing a prior theorem by Cai et al. and yielding increased efficiency through numerical studies. Moreover, we apply the CTMC framework to offer Laplace transforms for options priced against multifactor Markov processes. However, the additional factors increase the complexity of the price calculation. Specifically, we show that for two-factor CTMCs, the Laplace transform can be computed via reformulated forward and backward equations with modified boundary conditions at the origin and infinity respectively. Notably, the proposed price for the two-factor case is expressed in a closed form as a product of two independent entities, resembling the price for a one-factor CTMC. Consequently, the CTMC framework's advantages provide the basis for a comprehensive analysis of the effects of additional factors on the Laplace transforms. Lastly, we illustrate the practical application of the two-factor results by deriving Laplace transforms for call and put options priced against a time-changed CTMC. This time-change technique has far-reaching implications and can be used in conjunction with other time-changed models such as time-changed CIR or Merton models. Furthermore, we offer the numerical study of time-changed models by employing the inverse Laplace transform in a separate section. The accompanying software is available at https://github.com/MaxwellBosch/priceAsianOptions/tree/master/priceAsianOptions. Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, and revealing details about the spectra of these heavy degrees of freedom. Moreover, the stress on the inflationary potential due to these primordial features leads to an additional contribution to the primordial power spectrum. Our investigation is centered on oscillatory features in a single field inflationary model, where the properties of the massive field itself, the spectra of heavy modes, and the potential's shape can be deduced from the data, including the power spectrum and the non-Gaussian patterns generated by the higher mass-terms. Furthermore, a method for reconstructing the inflationary potential is also presented. This approach can be applied to other types of primordial features to investigate their effects on the primordial power spectrum and non-Gaussian patterns in a comprehensive manner. The backbending feature, a characteristic of deformed models undergoing a period of slow growth during inflation, is another case studied through this method. Lastly, a theoretical interpretation of the most recent primordial features observations in CMB data will be provided. The observation of classical cosmic fluctuations in heavy particles could become accessible in CMB data with improved precision, facilitating a deeper understanding of these phenomena and their connection to fundamental particle physics. The concept of cosmic parton physics, a modern extension of this connection, is also discussed. In particular, theories with a strong quantum connection to inflationary models, such as group field theory and dissipative quantum cosmology, are explored, allowing for the extraction of particle mass information. The effects of non-linear dispersion relations on scale based features in these cases are also considered. In total, a broad range of fundamental particle physics connections to inflationary models and their primordial features are examined, accompanied by a collection of open questions. Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe their internal workings in plain text. By using generic image data, this approach creates a link between visual and semantic information, allowing for its application across different domains without explicit labels. The LaViSE framework has a flexible structure, making it possible to analyze any network, regardless of whether its training data is accessible. Moreover, this technique can produce new explanations that go beyond the categories initially learned during training. It also has a significant application in discovering biases within datasets without needing additional labels. To facilitate further research, the framework, datasets, and code are openly available. When tested, LaViSE outperformed comparable methods, demonstrating its effectiveness in providing visual and textual insights into what networks have learned. Moreover, a deeper analysis was conducted using LaViSE to investigate the underlying biases present within the MS-COCO dataset. It was found that networks trained on this dataset exhibit substantial bias towards working with objects rather than their surroundings, and this bias also affects their ability to perform well even when given partial visual data. To gain even more visual insights, a new LaViSE variant called LaViSE-Vision is proposed, allowing for the quantitative analysis of the visual components that networks consider important, and revealing that there is a notable connection between this bias and the relative importance assigned to different visual elements. For instance, in the case of the Bird class within the MS-COCO dataset, it was found that networks placed greater importance to visual elements containing the class name rather than its non-visual components such as sounds or eggs. Therefore, a deeper reflection is encouraged regarding the nature of the bias present within the data and the development of methods to mitigate its effects. Ultimately, based on the results from a large analysis, it was discovered that networks trained on the COCO dataset exhibit a significant bias towards working with images containing humans rather than those without humans, and this bias also affects their ability to perform well even when given partial visual data. By comparing our simulation results with a recent photoemission spectroscopy study of one-dimensional cuprate chains, we discovered that long-range electron-phonon coupling, which goes beyond standard models, significantly affects the interaction between neighboring electrons. Within reasonable limits of this interaction and phonon energy, we observe a strong attraction between neighboring electrons, which is consistent with experimental findings. Additionally, we demonstrate that when the interaction is primarily repulsive, a strong attraction between neighboring electrons requires a lower phonon energy than when the interaction is attractive. Based on these findings, we suggest that a model incorporating long-range electron-phonon coupling, with an appropriate interaction and phonon energy, is well-suited for explaining the results of single-chain photoemission spectroscopy. Such a model provides a strong foundation for investigating the mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity in one-dimensional cuprate chains and other materials. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation for state-of-the-art achievements in this area lies in the application of predictive models derived from Bayesian neural networks. These advanced steganographic methods have achieved top-notch performance according to metrics such as PSNR, GR, and BLMS. It is crucial to note that the process of generating these models involves making critical decisions regarding the learning rate, Bayesian network structure, and the number of samples, each of which substantially impacts the predictive capacity of the associated Bayesian neural network. This work aims to find a systematic solution to these issues by developing a framework that integrates learning rate, predictive uncertainty, and Bayesian sparsity in a coherent framework. Our proposed model, $BNS\rightarrow BNN$, constitutes an advanced reversible steganographic method. A key distinguishing feature of this method lies in its ability to adaptively modify the predictive uncertainty of the learned predictive model as well as the blurriness of its associated likelihood distribution. The proposed method has achieved superior performance to the existing best approaches, demonstrating efficacy in preserving the intact appearance of the hidden message as well as the similarity between the cover and steganographic images. The method's source code is accessible via the following repository: https://github.com/fateme-pashae/BNS-to-BNN. Our implemented software utilizes Pytorch as the underlying programming framework. One of the additional advantages of the proposed method lies in its effortless capacity to switch from a robust, defeasible model to a more susceptible, non-defeasible one. This simple transition is feasible within a matter of seconds. As such, the proposed model offers a considerable amount of flexibility. Empirical results have also demonstrated that $BNS\rightarrow BNN$ possesses a lower computational footprint in comparison to the prevailing approaches. Our experiments revealed a computational latency ranging from 0.3-1.5 seconds for each image size from 512x512 to 2048x2048. Interestingly, the proposed method's computational efficiency is significantly greater than that of the prevailing approach while still achieving superior performance. This distinction in performance is likely rooted in several factors, including the incorporation of uncertainty and likelihood sparsity at the steganographic channel level. Furthermore, the proposed method's predictive model is trained using a larger number of samples in comparison to the existing approach. These two factors contribute to a notable improvement in performance. We strongly believe that these findings are pivotal in the development of future reversible steganographic methods. We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), where X is a Banach space. The inequality's solutions determine the boundedness of the resolvent R(λ,A) inside and outside the left half-plane and left invertibility of T, the C0-semigroup. We establish that for strongly stable T, the inequality's solutions are abundant, avoiding resonant λ in the left half-plane and ensuring strong stability of the resolvent R(λ,A). Conversely, we show minimal regularity of T can be obtained by ensuring high frequencies of non-zero solutions to the inequality. Our work focuses on exploring the Lyapunov inequality's power in establishing stability properties of T and of the operator A, extending traditional results. It also offers an alternative to well-known criteria like the Rabinowitz-Kato theorem and other regularity results. Our method is versatile, applicable to linear and, with restrictions, nonlinear settings. Ultimately, it offers a single tool to achieve key objectives. To enhance its utility, we offer four different formulations of the inequality, catering to diverse user preferences. Formulation 1 deals with bounded vs bounded below operators A. When the Banach space is a Hilbert space, we relate it to the adjoint (A*A)-1. Formulation 2 involves Galerkin-type methods for establishing stability of T. It demonstrates that these methods are powerful, obtaining regularity much more easily than usual. It also relates to the Thompson-Friedrich reduction. My preferred formulation is the fourth, where we relate the inequality to the Thompson-Friedrich reduction in a very explicit way. It involves projecting the operator A into the subspace U_1, where u_1 is a non-zero solution of the inequality. This is achieved using the perturbation (A-U_1) and some algebraic manipulation. Introducing a scalar is the only difference between this and the original inequality. Our work has a few limitations. It's focused on operators with closed graph, so we can't easily extend it to unbounded operators. It's also centered on the C0-semigroup, so we can't easily extend it to an analytic semigroup. Nevertheless, the tools we've developed are very useful in many cases and sometimes even in the cases that aren't covered by our theorem. For instance, we've applied this result to the regularity of the inverse of a multi-dimensional Wiener-Hopf integral operator

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we verify a long-standing conjecture of A. Magnus regarding these coefficients, making use of the Riemann-Hilbert and steepest descent methods in an unmodified form that applies to a function with poles at $x=1$. Additionally, the study determines the long-term behavior of the Christoffel-Darboux kernels associated with these orthogonal polynomials and investigates the asymptotic behavior of these polynomials. These findings are comparable to previous work of the authors on orthogonal polynomials with a logarithmic singularity at $x=0$. Furthermore, the study illustrates the applicability of these findings to a specific family of degree-$n$ real-root polynomials that have coefficients satisfying specific conditions and are known as the Stieltjes polynomials. It turns out these polynomials are a particular case of the logarithmic orthogonal polynomials when the logarithmic weight is modified to $\log\left(\frac{4k(1+x)}{1-x}\right)$. These polynomials have unique properties that support their use in approximation theory and theoretical physics. The study derives the asymptotic behavior of these polynomials using the obtained results for logarithmic orthogonal polynomials and verifies a conjectured formula for their coefficients proposed by A. Magnus that has not been previously published. These findings are comparable to the uncorrected linear asymptotics for logarithmic orthogonal polynomials and correct a correction made to the convergence theory for Stieltjes polynomials proposed by the first author. To prevent inaccurate annotations which could mislead automatic summarization systems, we develop a multi-stage recruitment process targeting high-quality MTurk workers. By establishing a rigorous evaluation pipeline, we demonstrate the ability to exclude unskilled workers before evaluation tasks are initiated, and subsequently collect reliable annotations while maintaining efficient resource allocation. The proposed approach serves as a model for selecting qualified annotators in other complex annotation endeavors. Furthermore, we investigate the efficacy of training task-specific instructions, evaluate various evaluation methodologies for detecting cheating, and study statistical properties of annotator performances, exploring such distributions from a statistical perspective. The approach to acquire top-tier human annotations for summarization is a two-step process. Initially, only a small subset of MTurk workers, representing random samples from a larger pool, are chosen to complete qualification tasks. Subsequently, full-length summarization evaluation tasks are assigned to these skilled annotators. We categorize our approach to recruit top-tier annotators into two primary types - 'filtering' and combining qualification and evaluation tasks and'refining' by keeping evaluation tasks separate from qualifications and leveraging various machine learning models to identify top-tier annotators based on their task-specific profiles.

In response to the intricacies of network data, a new type of hybrid network is suggested that blends rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  This hybrid network creates edges according to a mixture of these rules.  Specifically, when a new edge is added, it follows the preferential attachment rule with a certain probability and otherwise forms between two randomly selected nodes.  This approach leads to a distribution of node in- and out-degrees that has less extreme outliers compared to a purely preferential attachment network, thereby improving upon this traditional model.  Inference methods applicable to the new model are then proposed and demonstrated with both artificially generated and actual network data.  In comparison tests, the proposed network model outperforms the traditional one in terms of accuracy, especially for networks with more nodes.  Furthermore, the proposed network model holds a substantial advantage over a model that only uses uniform attachment when it comes to predictive accuracy.  In fact, the proposed network model's predictive accuracy surpasses that of a purely preferential attachment network.  In addition to statistical analysis, the proposed approach is shown to have lower Mean Squared Error in degree distribution forecasts.  The theoretical foundation of this new model is also discussed through an investigation into its fundamental characteristics.  The study further examines the characteristics of hybrid networks through a preliminary computation and offers suggestions for future research directions.  The main body of this study consists of ten pages and it includes a related figure and seven related tables.  The related code for implementing the proposed network model is available at https://github.com/felix-fang/dhbn-degrees.  The experimental data for the networks considered in this study can be found at https://github.com/felix-fang/network-data.  The accuracy of the proposed network model was also verified numerically through a solution to equations at https://mathematica.stackexchange.com/a/247469/46258.  A related list of acronyms and mathematical notation can also be found in the study.  In conclusion, the proposed network model demonstrates impressive results when applied to a panchgani school network, displaying its potential that this type of network model holds substantial value.  Eventually, the proposed network model may be able to explain the characteristics of the Facebook network, yet explaining this network remains an unsolved research question at the end of this study.  In addition to discussing the characteristics of hybrid networks, the proposed network model is shown to have numerous potential applications in degree distribution forecasting and network inference, which could greatly enhance their practical usability.

Countable, locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair of Steinitz numbers, consisting of one value which equals or exceeds 1. Each such algebra can be topologically equivalent to a countable Bernoulli algebra equipped with a countably infinite proximal structure. We demonstrate that such a structure is intrinsic to each measure algebra, providing a novel argument that relies on dynamical systems principles. Moreover, we show that a compact, zero-dimensional system possesses a free measure that makes system's action as a measure-preserving system a factor-automorphism only if that system is a shift space. Finally, we outline implicit, uncountable generalizations to the established principle that locally standard measure algebras are equivalent to Bernoulli algebras.

All AI systems inevitably make mistakes, characterized by their unpredictability and distinctness from human errors. A critical objective is to rectify these AI errors without compromising their established abilities and ideally without requiring direct human intervention. This report outlines an innovative approach aimed at boosting the cognitive capabilities of individual AI systems by collaborating with other AIs. It synthesizes insights from multi-agent learning systems and introduces novel mathematical techniques for non-recursive corrections of legacy AI errors. This study develops a foundational framework for non-destructive AI corrections and derives a sequence of probabilistic separation theorems, serving as a powerful tool for evaluating machine learning techniques and algorithms in complex dimensions. These theorems establish that, even with large data sets and in high dimensions, linear classifiers can effectively distinguish between incorrect and correct responses, providing a feasible solution to the long-standing "platoon" problem and facilitating augmented AI corrections. This study derives a general strategy for non-destructive AI corrections and presents a specific application to the challenging task of correcting a single Markov chain's predictions in a multi-class scenario. It is also demonstrated that, in the context of deep neural networks, our theorems provide explicit quantitative limits on the sample complexity of non-destructive corrections. These results open up potential advancements in using multi-agent collaborations to drive self-improvement within the field of artificial general intelligence. It is also proposed that this concept could lead to breakthroughs in the capacity for collective self-improvement, and that a collective collective alignment of collective AI systems with human values could become a feasible possibility. Following an initial testing phase, this study is now in a position to recommend the deployment of a collective alignment strategy for the development of more advanced AI systems. Recommendations are provided for the effective design and evaluation of collective AI approaches. This study is accompanied by a series of educational videos that explain the theoretical concepts. It is anticipated that its findings will facilitate advancements in the field of artificial general intelligence and the development of collective AI systems. Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. This method effectively leverages a combination of two techniques: soft parameter pruning through optimal transportation and hard parameter sparsification during forward passes. This dynamic balance enables initial exploration of various sparsity patterns and gradually shifts towards optimizing parameters with respect to a predetermined sparsity pattern. Spartan offers flexibility in incorporating diverse sparsity policies, encompassing both random and structured sparsity, as well as cost functions that can be tailored to address memory constraints. Spartan demonstrates exceptional performance on ImageNet-1K classification, achieving significant sparsity in ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 models while maintaining accuracy within 1% of their fully dense counterparts. This performance is further enhanced by leveraging knowledge distilled from sparse models, which can reach accuracy on par with fully dense models while achieving sparsity of 85% in the ResNet-50 model. To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as a function of low temperature and reduced tunneling height, it has a lower temperature threshold for exponential increase compared to a setup with low-resistance electrodes, and its peak width also changes with height. On the other hand, non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks won't survive a low-resistance-to-high-resistance switch, and upon re-establishing the low-resistance electrode, any temperature-related shifts in zero-energy peaks can be quantitatively identified and explained. Our experimental design aims to explore this concept. Future experiments with a variety of tunneling heights will help validate this technique. The experiments discussed within this report have been conducted. The resulting data suggests that tunneling conductance through a high-resistance electrode preserves the essential characteristics of Majorana peaks, and upon re-establishing the low-resistance electrode, non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks were observed that exhibited a 2.9 millielectronvolt peak shift with increasing height from contact 1 to contact 4. However, a major complication was discovered which threatens the technique: an unanticipated series of high-velocity features within the tunneling conductance. We have established a non-asymptotic lower bound for the eigenvalues of a design matrix, generated by linear bandit algorithms that incur sub-linear regret in action spaces with constant curvature. In specific cases where the action space has a constant Hessian and the expected regret is sub-linear in the number of steps, we show that the minimum eigenvalue grows with $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ for large $n$. In contrast to previous lower bounds with tighter rates, this result applies more broadly to any algorithm using a fixed exploration strategy, thus separating upper and lower bounds for both Bayesian and non-Bayesian settings. Moreover, our analysis reveals a reduction factor in the eigenvalue growth that increases with the dimensionality of the action space, indicating a shift in the bandit phase from exploration-dominated to exploitation-dominated. To prove these results, we use a new non-asymptotic lower bound for the eigenvalues of $\ell_2$-regularized empirical risk minimization (Ridge regression) that applies to any model with Lipschitz effects and bounded second-order derivatives, thus going beyond the context of linear bandits. In addition, under certain conditions applicable to Bayesian linear/linear-threshold bandits with scalar actions and geometric action spaces, we obtain an improved non-asymptotic lower bound for the spectral risk ratio that applies to the ridge estimator, thereby generalizing our previous work and providing a separate problem. Ultimately, these findings are pivotal in confirming a shift in the ridge regression bias-variance phase that increases with the dimensionality for a significant class of models, thus yielding new insights into the reliability of statistical algorithms used in the machine learning community. Moreover, our analysis has significant implications for the bandit community as a whole, given its generalizability to the Bayesian setting and the (asymptotic) non-Bayesian setting, thus rendering the lower bound applicable to any algorithm fixing the exploration schedule. In addition to these results, which are complementary in their (partially) non-Bayesian applicability, we obtained an additional convergence bound for the spectral risk ratio with the ridge regressor in the context of Bayesian threshold bandits, thus constituting an independent problem with further advancements. Specifically, our analysis reveals a reduction factor in the risk difference that decreases exponentially with the number of samples, thus indicating a shift in the threshold bandit phase from exploration-dominated to estimation-dominated, but with a different rate, given the presence of an additional non-linear effect. Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, where different types of electron flows, determined by specific indices, are observed.  Our research, however, demonstrates that this effect can be more accurately described by the orbital Hall effect, where the indices representing "valleys" are replaced with a distinct physical property called the orbital magnetic moment, capable of being applied consistently across the entire range of the Brillouin zone.  Utilizing the parameters of the band structure, the orbital Hall effect is shown to be distinct from the valley Hall effect, and revealed through its connection with the anomalous Nernst effect.  Our research also uncovers the relationship between the directions of the orbital magnetic moment and the symmetry of the system, as well as developing an inequality that describes the total dissipation rate.  Our findings are further substantiated by applying the orbital Hall effect to gapless Dirac and Weyl lattices.  Our research proposes a method for experimentally verifying the orbital Hall effect by measuring the longitudinal electrical resistance in response to a magnetic field and an applied torque.  Our predictions indicate that this effect should be observable in systems engineered from twisted monolayers, and naturally occurring bilayers.  Our research demonstrates that the emergence of the orbital Hall effect arises naturally from the combination of a magnetic field, symmetry, and geometry.  Our findings are further substantiated by showing its connection to the emergence of fractional orbital Hall effects in systems of Coulomb interactions, as well as the possibility of observing the orbital Hall effect through experiments involving thermal gradients and torsional oscillations.  Our predictions indicate that these effects should be observable in materials such as twisted graphene bilayers, and naturally occurring trilayers.  Our research provides a framework for linking the emergence of fractional orbital Hall effects to various stacking configurations through the geometric principle.  Our findings are further substantiated by demonstrating the potential to construct, manipulate and study the fractional orbital Hall effects in systems engineered from twisted monolayers.  Our research shows that these effects arise from delicate balances between the effects of stacking, geometry, and orbital motion, and can be used to develop innovative strategies for quantitatively understanding the interplay between these principles at the atomic level.  Our predictions indicate that these strategies should be applicable to a broad range of materials and systems.  Our research provides a new path for linking the emergence of orbital motions to the emergence of collective phenomena, and demonstrates its potential to pave the way for a more comprehensive understanding of orbital contributions at the atomic level. The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to inaccuracies when objects of different brightness are mistaken for the same source. However, incorporating the magnitudes of sources can rectify this issue and improve accuracy. A novel approach described here utilizes photometric data from multiple catalogs to determine which sources likely belong to the same object. This involves using a type of probability map called a multivariate normal distribution, based on the differences in magnitudes and directions of sources. The method is tested on a simulated dataset and a real one, showcasing its benefits. When applied to a set of catalogs for the Large Millimeter Telescope, this method reduced the number of incorrect matches from 17.4% to 9.8%. Notably, using magnitudes alone would have only decreased the errors to 13.4%. Additionally, the method appears to perform well when applied to a real dataset of catalogs, indicating its practical applicability, and it is noted that some incorrect matches are due to unaccounted for noise in the data. A method to handle this noise based on a set of high-confidence matches would improve accuracy even further, potentially lowering the number of incorrect matches to less than 5%. This approach is set to become a standard procedure for processing data for the Large Millimeter Telescopes at Big Island and Yebes, as well as other similar surveys. Its implementation in a shared code repository includes provisions for easy distribution and further modifications. The repository uses a name that reflects the method's purpose: LMT_Catalog_Match_phot. In this paper, a hypergraph is considered as the family of its edges, and a hypergraph is said to possess property C(k, ρ) if the size of the intersection of all its subgraph covers exceeds k*ρ, where k and ρ are positive integers, and the intersection is taken over all subsets of its vertices. A vertex cover of a hypergraph is a subset of its vertices that covers all its edges. We establish that for every pair of positive integers k and ρ, a hypergraph possessing property C(k, ρ) and having at most ρ^3k vertices cannot be covered by the k-th minimal vertex cover. Furthermore, for any given pair of positive integers q and r, a graph possessing property C(q, r) cannot be covered by the r-th minimal vertex cover, and this solution is optimal as it refrains from setting a upper limit on its vertex count. A long-debated conjecture regarding the covering number of generalized Petersen graphs is also validated here, and several open questions are proposed in the text.
