Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation methods predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. Through a user study involving domain experts, we compared OntoPlot's usability to that of Protégé, the industry-standard ontology editor, finding that OntoPlot surpassed expectations in facilitating association-related tasks and earned widespread endorsement from domain specialists. This study underscores OntoPlot's potential as a pioneering tool for exploring and working with ontologies featuring non-hierarchical associations. Ultimately, OntoPlot aims to foster greater use and working with ontologies featuring multiple types of associations. The system can be freely demonstrated at https://onto-plot.net. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-text representation through a shared neural network, whereas CycleGAN leverages cycle-consistency and identity mapping to preserve input characteristics after cross-domain conversion. As both approaches can train end-to-end models with unpaired data, we leverage their strengths to improve the speech-text mapping and shared representation, ultimately enhancing speech-to-text performance. Our experimental findings on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets reveal significant reductions in character error rate (approximately 8-13%), surpassing the baseline performance and demonstrating comparable results with fully supervised systems. Moreover, we found that the training process preserves the integrity of speech-text mappings across various datasets. Our code has been made available on GitHub for public reference. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. This formulation can be translated into a type of machine learning known as active inference, which can be used to develop autonomous robotic systems utilizing deep learning techniques. A crucial step in this framework involves creating a mental framework distinguishing self from environment. If this self-differentiation step is skipped, the robot may incorrectly construct its mental framework, potentially leading to uncertain world representations. We demonstrate numerical and experimental evidence showing that missing this step results in inconsistent self-representations. Furthermore, navigation tasks in a virtual environment rely on a detailed and accurate mental framework to make informed decisions. Without adequate self-differentiation, the robot may resort to relying solely on sensory data, omitting the incorporation of prior knowledge to form a complete picture of the world. This study highlights critical consequences when implementing active inference for autonomous robot systems and suggests effective strategies for accurate world modeling. Leveraging the capabilities of the C++ programming language in conjunction with the Tensorflow and BayesNet libraries allows for both efficient active inference modeling and speedy training. Utilizing deep active inference can provide an unparalleled level of autonomy for robotic systems, empowering them to intelligently interact with their surroundings. Future research can focus on integrating multi-sensor robotic systems within this framework, complemented by the development of standardized techniques for active inference modeling. Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations out of equilibrium to explore the Soret effect, particularly the influence of flexible molecules' internal freedom on this phenomenon. As we softened the molecules, we found the thermal diffusion coefficient to decrease and change its direction, and we attributed these findings to two potential factors: temperature-induced conformational changes causing bulkier structures to move to the warmer area; and asymmetry in interactions between flexible and rigid molecules, which leads to increased movement of flexible molecules in response to the warmer conditions. To better understand these soft molecules, we used a model to analyse the contributing factors, which revealed that internal degrees of freedom significantly impact thermal diffusion. When these internal degrees of freedom are maximally excited, they contribute 70% of the total thermal diffusion. The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective evaluation by an NLP model depends on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in cases where the writing quality is subpar. Despite the current prominence of large transformer-based models in various NLP applications, these models' computational complexity poses significant practical limitations to their deployment. This paper sets out to dispute the prevailing notion that larger models necessarily lead to better performance in Automated Essay Scoring. To this end, the study assesses the capabilities of multiple NLP models with fewer parameters that were fine-tuned on an AES dataset and demonstrates superior results can be achieved by combining these models' outputs, thereby reducing the total number of required parameters. Additionally, the study explores an unexplored aspect of AES – its sensitivity to writing quality. By treating AES as a noise-sensitive operation, the study leverages tools from statistical inference to quantify the impact of model noise on its output. Consequently, the study's findings offer guidance on striking the right balance between the accuracy of Automated Essay Scores and the computational resources required to achieve them. Ultimately, the study's outcomes have the potential to pave the way for the widespread adoption of NLP models with fewer parameters in real-world AES applications, and the concept of treating such systems as noise-sensitive operations. These results and tools can be utilized to devise more effective AES systems. Finally, the study's analysis suggests that the current limitations of modern AES systems stem from their inability to tap into the underlying essence of human creativity, an aspect NLP models are not yet capable of capturing. Therefore, the study raises a fundamental question – what precisely constitutes creativity? The study's answers to these questions are set out below in the individual paper's sections.

Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the transfer of knowledge across various tasks. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the challenge of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study provides effective, sample-efficient methods to address the dual problems of learning a shared feature set from related tasks and transferring this knowledge to unseen tasks. This work sheds light on the central issue of meta-learning. Furthermore, we present theoretical limits on the minimum sample size required to learn these linear representations. In contrast to existing research, our study is focused on linear regression rather than the classification of binary tasks. Additionally, we extend our findings to a 'hub-and-spokes' scenario where one task is more informative than the others. Our conclusions are verified by analytical proofs and numerical simulations. To the best of our knowledge, this study initiates the exploration of meta-learning algorithms backed by theoretical foundations in the domain of representation learning. Our research offers a valuable stepping stone for studying the representation of non-linear models, which poses an highly complex problem. Our work shares some similarities with a recent study by Garg et al. (2020) but differs significantly, as our research is focused on a more general problem, is less assumption-dependent and considers an overarching scenario. In contrast, their work investigates a specific 'hub-and-spokes' scenario and is supported by a distributionally robust optimization approach. In summary, our research offers a starting point for the study of representation learning in the context of meta-learning and initiates the exploration of theoretical validity of meta-learning algorithms. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method to create high-performance yet lightweight models. This study initially assesses its application in compressing MT models, particularly for languages with scarce training data, examining eight languages in the process. Notably, it's discovered that distillation-based model performance variability heavily relies on several preconditions, making it a somewhat unreliable compression approach. To improve on this, we explore post-training quantization as a means to compress these models. Ultimately, while distillation was found effective in certain low-resource languages, it's shown that quantization produces more consistent performance outcomes across a broader range of languages, particularly those with the least available training data. Therefore, we recommend considering multiple compression approaches in order to produce a lightweight model for languages with scarce training data. Lastly, based on existing research, we create a distillation-based compression pipeline that allows for the creation of small, effective MT models for various languages. However, a separate investigation is required to develop adapted models that combine the capabilities of pre-training multilingual learning and compression, given that these are complementary research areas. This investigation is necessary in order to develop a unified pipeline that is required for successful model deployment in compression. To initiate this investigation, we analyze the impact of different compression methods on pre-trained multilingual models, discovering that distillation generally produces more consistent performance variability in compression. Subsequently, we propose improving upon distillation-based model performance variability in compression by optimizing certain key prerequisites. To initiate this investigation, we analyze the predictions produced by the multilingual models on English-Dutch and English-French translation datasets, using the wordspace kits which are widely utilized in the field as the basis for our investigation. Ultimately, our findings indicate that by improving upon these prerequisites through various methods such as enhancing annealing, reducing teacher-overlapping, decreasing data-overlapping, and controlling batch-size, we can consistently achieve consistent distillation-based model performance across various scenarios. Consequently, these findings can subsequently be applied to other research areas in order to improve upon model performance variability. Ultimately, our investigation leads to the creation of a unified pipeline in compression, revealing that while distillation was found effective in certain low-resource languages, it's shown that quantization produces more consistent performance outcomes across a broader range of languages, leading to the creation of a distillation-based compression pipeline that is required for successful model deployment

The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that the set of possible Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs is infinite, and for 3-uniform graphs, Friedler et al. demonstrated a subset of those densities is irrational, but for single hypergraphs, this result was previously uncertain. The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms in identifying abnormalities on chest X-rays is limited by the laborious task of gathering and annotating training data. To alleviate this issue, we explore how image enhancement techniques can lower the necessity for labelled data in chest X-ray pneumonia detection through semantic segmentation. By training fully convolutional neural network models on subsets of various sizes from a total dataset, each model undergoes a different image enhancement while its performance is compared to a baseline model trained without such augmentations on the entire dataset. Ultimately, we discovered that using rotate and mixup image enhancement methods leads to a significant reduction of 70% in labelled data requirements while maintaining comparable performance to the baseline model in AUC score and Dice coefficient. Moreover, by combining all augmentations, the model exhibited improved performance (+2.3% in AUC score and +3.4% in Dice score) over the baseline model. Furthermore, to make these augmentations effective across a variety of unlabelled test images, an adaptation of U-Net architecture with self-training strategy is proposed. This approach enables the application of image enhancement techniques to both training and testing data, resulting in an average AUC score improvement of +1.3% over the baseline model. Consequently, the proposed method is seen to offer substantial time savings in data labelling. Nevertheless, despite the decreased necessity for labelled data, cross-domain generalisability of the model remains a challenge, specifically when there's a difference in data distribution between a training set and a testing set (e.g. between pneumonia dataset and a radiograph dataset). To address this, an adaptation of the LEAP objective function is proposed to enhance convergence of the model during test-time domain adaptation. Consequently, the test-time domain adaptation strategy results in a notable improvement of +5.6% in AUC score over the baseline model. The experimental outcome also demonstrates that with domain adaptation, the requirements for labelled data can be lowered by as much as 60%. To facilitate replication and evaluation of these findings, the code and dataset used in the experiments are made accessible on github at https://github.com/jayvee/Reducing_Labeled_Data_Requirement_for_pneumonia_segmentation. This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations akin to those by Coleman and Gurtin, further subject to dynamic boundary conditions with memory. These systems contain nonlinear elements situated both internally and on the boundary, with their behavior either dictated by classical dissipation principles or falling under the realm of non-equilibrium theories. Moreover, we allow for disparate memory kernels between the interior and boundary of the domain. Consequently, we establish a broad framework for solving such systems, with an emphasis on a method using maximal monotone operators, thus effectively obtaining estimates of the solution in a chosen norm without relying on differentiating the solution. Moreover, we demonstrate that the solution continuously depends on various parameters such as the memory kernels and boundary conditions. Ultimately, we present some test examples of systems with specific nonlinear elements and examine their associated well-posedness properties. These examples include systems related to traditional heat conduction equations under dynamic boundary conditions, providing new insights into their behavior. The presented methods are likely to be applicable to a much broader class of problems. This work is a part of a larger series of larger projects aimed at developing comprehensive frameworks for heat conduction equations, now complete, and extending to systems with fluid motion in the near future. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine radiology. However, certain pathological conditions (such as spinal deformities and vertebral body tumors) significantly hinder the process by distorting vertebral appearance. The video sequence of vertebral bodies, captured through image reconstruction technology, is used to establish a baseline for vertebrae localization and identification in CT scans. By initially extracting regional features and reducing complexity through dimensionality reduction, a vertebra is initially detected. Following this, a model of contorted vertebral bodies is established and used to determine the vertebral body's corrected position. By correcting the vertebral body's position, a more accurate estimate of its original X-ray density is obtained, enabling the identification of C1. A novel, anatomically-based optimization technique is developed to simultaneously calculate the vertebral position's correction and the vertebra's orientation. By applying this new technique to a test case, a notable improvement of at least 3% has been observed when compared to the current state-of-the-art. Furthermore, a significant decrease in computation time of approximately 9.5s has been achieved compared to the current fastest method, while using fewer parameters. By leveraging a dataset consisting of 100 subjects with severe spinal deformities and vertebral body tumors, it was observed that the proposed technique successfully localized and identified all vertebral bodies. Consequently, the proposed technique has been successfully tested on a diverse set of pathological cases. As a result of accurate localization and identification, the proposed technique has enabled the precise calculation of spine segment parameters. By applying a statistical model, the proposed technique was evaluated on a set of pathological subjects, yielding a performance that closely matches a current gold standard. More specifically, the proposed technique achieved a performance within 99.8% of the current best technique. Furthermore, the proposed technique achieved a performance within 99.5% of the current best technique when tested on a set of subjects with severe spinal deformities, indicating a notable result. A major drawback of the current best technique is the failure to accurately localize and identify vertebral bodies in certain pathological cases, resulting in a significant loss of accuracy. In contrast, the proposed technique has successfully overcome this limitation by accurately localizing and identifying vertebral bodies in a diverse set of pathological cases through the development of an anatomically-based optimization technique that accurately calculates vertebral body properties. More specifically, the proposed technique applied a novel technique to calculate the vertebral body's Apparent X-ray Density by accurately correcting the vertebral body's position.

A well-documented phenomenon, microtearing modes, occurs due to the electron temperature gradient in a plasma and causes fine-scale magnetic reconnections and the formation of magnetic islands. Prior research in a slab geometry setting showed that the drive mechanism requires collisions, but our simulations show that in the absence of collisions, there is still a small-scale electron temperature fluctuation linked to the mode. Utilizing quasi-linear theory to analyze this phenomenon, we find that the small-scale modes persist even without collisions and that their growth rates are in line with those seen in simulations. Furthermore, we discovered that the mode requires a minimum electron mean-free path, indicating that as a system becomes increasingly collisionless, the associated temperature fluctuations decrease, affecting the mode's behavior. This work, performed using the VENUS magnetic reconnection code, explores the properties of small-scale modes in both linear and non-linear regimes, and demonstrates that the modes continue to form and grow into larger structures in both cases. In particular, our analysis reveals that the linear regime allows for a smaller maximum wavenumber than in non-linear regimes, considering that the largest modes observed in simulations are influenced by numerical effects. Lastly, our simulations of non-linear regimes reveal that the largest possible wavenumber scales with the number of grid points used. As applied to solar physics, our study implies that in areas of high flow velocity or intense radio emission, we can expect microtearing modes to drive reconnection and island formation, resulting in a wider separation between magnetic field parcels. More specifically, in coronal shear flows, these islands could contribute to the formation of parasitic arch structures observed in solar physics, and in the Sun's polar regions, these islands could be a source of power for solar flares. Furthermore, in the Earth's magnetosphere, these island formations may contribute to the relaxation of magnetic fields. Finally, these results have significant implications for understanding various astrophysical phenomena, including those mentioned above. But in the case of very high temperatures, these island formations may not be possible. For instance, in the case of $T_e<4000$K, these island formations may not occur, which explains why we see small-scale reconnection only in the Earth's magnetotail, where the temperature is naturally low. In summary, these results help to further our understanding of astrophysical plasma behavior and serve as a valuable tool for checking and validating theoretical models in the field of astrophysical plasma science. A surge in demand for search by image has led researchers to investigate fashion instance-level image retrieval, which involves finding matching images. Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables users to search not only identical items but also similar clothes with distinct attributes. However, this task is challenging due to the difficulty in defining attributes and preserving query uniqueness. Although fashion instance-level image retrieval and fashion attribute manipulation are crucial in real-world applications, most studies have focused on one problem alone. This paper presents a novel framework for fashion image retrieval by combining these two tasks. The proposed framework, called semi-supervised feature-level attribute manipulation, uses a hybrid approach. It employs a GAN-based model in the feature level to change attributes while maintaining the identity of the query image, while utilizing memory-based information to guide this process. The framework outperforms baselines on two datasets by a significant margin, with an impressive 6.7% improvement over the best comparison model on the NIST dataset. The framework's efficacy is showcased through a virtual fashion retailer application, providing users with manipulated images displaying how a shirt might look in a different color. Constructing the matching cost is a critical step in estimating light field depth but has received limited attention in the era of deep learning. The prevailing method in the field of deep learning constructs matching cost through the sequential shifting of each sub-aperture image with predefined offsets, making the process intricate and labor-intensive. This complexity stems from the necessity of carefully selecting the extent of shifts, feasible offsets, and a balanced weighted system to ensure a robust reconstruction. 

Our research presents an innovative, efficient matching cost constructor specifically tailored for deep learning-based light field depth estimation. This constructor first applies an und-warped map to create a distorted version of each sub-aperture image, and then uses a hierarchical keypoint search strategy to determine the optimal displacement for each pixel across the 2D displacement search grid. 

A unique one-sided similarity measurement is proposed to quickly and accurately identify the optimal displacement for each pixel. Consequently, our constructor requires minimal shifting steps during the optimization process, making it easier to couple with deep learning techniques. In experiments, our proposed constructor outperforms its predecessors by delivering superior quantitative results on the established "Living-room" benchmark as well as the newly formed "Dragon Boat" benchmark inspired by "Mythical Creatures". This constructor also facilitates a notable reduction in optimization iterations when paired with a state-of-the-art depth estimation network.
